- Mid-rolls: the review said ads \"will be placed\" inside the story by default. The page says automatic slots are the default only once mid-rolls are turned on, and \"Ad slots are not guaranteed to serve ads.\" Mid-rolls are also set per video, not only as a channel default.
- Spam: the kit's \"no music changes\" is about calm sound within one video. YouTube's example is the same track across many videos.
- Phone limit: \"cannot post at all\" became \"cannot post its full-length videos\" (videos of 15 minutes or less still upload). The added check that advanced access also starts with phone verification confirms there is no way around it.
- \"Features that require a phone verification\" isn't wording on the page. The page says \"You’ll see “Enabled” next to the features you have access to.\"
- Reused content: \"would make the channel ineligible\" became the page's \"monetization may be removed\". The first script mentions the Rule of Benedict; it doesn't quote it.
- Ads before YPP: the page doesn't say where those ads appear, so \"in its stories\" was dropped.
- AI disclosure: the four must-disclose bullets don't name a stock AI narrator, but the page's general rule (\"disclose AI-generated or altered content that seems realistic\") is broad, and YouTube may label AI content automatically. The action now says to choose Yes when unsure.
- Made for kids: \"cartoon-style thumbnails\" became cartoon characters, matching the page's factor. I also added that a YouTube override can only be appealed.

Two things remain third-party only. The reviewer's \"July 2026\" date for YouTube reworking its inauthentic-content guidance rests on news sites. The official page's only dated entry on this is July 15, 2025, when \"repetitious content\" was renamed \"inauthentic content\". The page's current sections match what those sites describe. Any claim that YouTube targets faceless channels as such is not official.

The YPP notes check out on https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851: \"Have advanced features access on YouTube\"; 4,000 qualified watch hours from public long-form videos in 12 months with 1,000 subscribers. Private, unlisted and deleted videos, ad campaigns, Shorts, and livestreams that are unlisted, deleted or not converted to VOD don't count.

review.audience_setting: Not made for kids. YouTube's Help Center says: "General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn't intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as 'not made for kids.'" Historic crime told from court records is meant for teens and adults. The illustrations don't change this, because YouTube lists "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as general audience. Set it for the whole channel and for each upload, and keep kid-targeted words and characters out of titles, tags and thumbnails.

findings.topic: Doxxing: addresses and phone numbers in court files, police reports and newspaper scans
findings.official_quote: Content that shares, threatens to share, or encourages others to share non-public personally identifiable information (PII). ... PII includes, but isn’t limited to, home addresses; email addresses; sign-in credentials, like a username or password; phone numbers; passport numbers; medical records; bank account information; or the name of a school a minor attends. (Harassment policy.) The EDSA page also lists among content that may not get an exception: "Content that reveals an individual’s private information, such as their home address, email addresses, sign-in credentials, phone numbers, passport number, or bank account information (doxxing)"
findings.applies: The whole channel is built on primary documents: court files, police reports, FBI files and newspapers. These often print home addresses, phone numbers and account details of defendants, witnesses, tipsters and victims. This matters most for recent cases with living people: Hatton Garden (2015), Antwerp (2003), the Gardner heist (1990) and the D. B. Cooper files, which name many tipsters and suspects. Doxxing is on YouTube's list of content that may not get an EDSA exception, so a 'documentary' framing does not save a video that shows an address on screen.
findings.action: Before any document or news clipping goes on screen, blur every home address, phone number, account number and ID number, and any minor's school. Do this even for people who died long ago, and even if the page is already online somewhere, unless it is clearly 'widely available public information' such as a business address.

findings.topic: Real people in mugshots and photos: privacy complaints, including from families of the dead
findings.official_quote: We also consider public interest, newsworthiness, consent, and whether the information is otherwise publicly available. ... A close family member makes the claim for a deceased individual. ... If we remove your video for a privacy violation, do not upload another version featuring the same people.
findings.applies: Mugshots, custody photos and newspaper portraits show 'uniquely identifiable' people. Some are alive, such as Hatton Garden gang members, members of the Antwerp ring and Gardner Museum guards. Others are dead but have close family who can complain, such as Great Train Robbery defendants and the injured train driver's family. A convicted defendant in a famous case has strong 'public interest, newsworthiness' weight. Relatives, bystanders, jurors and acquitted or never-charged people do not. YouTube's process lets the creator 'use the Trim or Blur tools in YouTube Studio' before it reviews, and making the video private does not count as a fix.
findings.action: Show faces only of people central to the documented case: convicted people and officials acting in their role. Blur or leave out relatives, bystanders, witnesses and never-charged suspects. If a privacy complaint comes in, trim or blur the person within the deadline YouTube gives, and never re-upload a removed video with the same people.

findings.topic: Unsolved cases and suspects: defamation, and no ads for 'slander and defamation'
findings.official_quote: Malicious personal attacks, slander, and defamation. (Advertiser-friendly guidelines, 'This content will receive no ad earnings'.) YouTube's Defamation page: "We take into account local legal considerations in our defamation blocking process, and in some cases, we require a court order."
findings.applies: 'D. B. Cooper: What the Files Actually Say' and 'The Gardner Museum Heist' are unsolved. The FBI files name people who were never charged, and some of them or their families are alive. Hatton Garden, the Great Train Robbery and Piltdown are British stories, and YouTube applies 'local legal considerations' when deciding whether to block a video in a country. The kit's promise of 'No guessing about guilt' is exactly the right protection. The risk is breaking it in a script.
findings.action: In unsolved cases, describe named people only as the record does ('the FBI investigated X; X was never charged'), with the source on screen. Never say or suggest guilt beyond a conviction. Keep thumbnails and titles free of an uncharged person's face or name.

findings.topic: Crime documentaries can earn ads; how-to detail and bare CCTV of break-ins earn none
findings.official_quote: Documentaries about crime. (listed under 'This content can earn ad revenue') ... Content meant to educate viewers on how to gain unauthorized access or make unauthorized changes to systems, devices, or property in malicious ways. ... Displaying a house break-in without additional context, e.g. CCTV footage of a house break-in. (listed under 'This content will receive no ad earnings')
findings.applies: Six of the ten titles are heists or thefts. The Mona Lisa script ends 'Next: how he got it out of the building.' Hatton Garden (drilling into a vault) and Antwerp (getting past vault security) invite technical walk-throughs, and the Metropolitan Police published CCTV of the Hatton Garden gang. A history told as a story is in the ad-earning column. A step-by-step method for beating locks, alarms or vaults, or CCTV with no narration, is in the no-ads column. The Community Guidelines also ban 'Instructional theft videos posted with the express intent to steal physical goods or get something for free' (Harmful or dangerous content policy), which a history channel won't do by accident, but it shows where the line is.
findings.action: Tell the method at story level: what happened, why it worked in that year, and how the thieves were caught. Leave out reusable technical specifics such as tool models, alarm defeat steps and vault layouts. Always narrate over CCTV or police footage, and never frame thieves as role models ('genius', 'legend', 'how to').

findings.topic: Violence, injuries and crime-scene images: ad limits, and context must be in the video
findings.official_quote: Content where the focal point is on blood, violence, or injury, when presented without other context, is not suitable for advertising. ... A documentary on a recent homicide featuring descriptive language of the circumstances of death. (limited ad earnings) ... Focus on blood, guts, gore, bodily fluids (human or animal), crime scenes or accident photos with little to no context. (no ad earnings). Violent or graphic content policy: "For educational content containing the kinds of violent or graphic content noted above, this context must appear in the images or audio of the video itself. Providing it in the title or description is insufficient."
findings.applies: Most of the ten titles involve little violence. The exceptions: the Great Train Robbery, where the driver was struck and injured; D. B. Cooper, an air hijacking; and the description's word 'disappearances', which can lead to deaths. YouTube's EDSA page says it 'may not make EDSA exceptions for context that may be in comments, tags, channel descriptions, pinned comments, or other surfaces'. So the kit's good promise of 'no graphic detail for its own sake' protects nothing unless each video's narration carries it. The Harassment policy also bans 'Content reveling in or mocking the death or serious injury of an identifiable individual.'
findings.action: Describe injuries and deaths briefly and without graphic detail. Never put crime-scene, injury or body photos in thumbnails or on screen. Say the who, when, where and why aloud in the narration, and never treat a victim's injury as part of the 'fun' of a heist.

findings.topic: Mugshots, newspaper scans and archive photos: copyright; a credit is not a licence
findings.official_quote: Ultimately, it's your responsibility to verify that a work is in the public domain before you upload it to YouTube. ... For example, works created by U.S. government agencies are automatically in the public domain. (Copyright on YouTube.) Copyright myths: "Giving credit to the copyright owner doesn’t automatically give you the rights to use their copyrighted content."
findings.applies: The description promises 'Sources are listed under every video', which is good for trust, but YouTube says crediting does not give rights. The dispute page also lists 'Giving credit to the copyright owner' among reasons that are 'NOT legitimate reasons to dispute a claim'. FBI material, such as the D. B. Cooper files and sketches, falls under YouTube's 'U.S. government agencies' example. Press photos and news-agency archive images from 1963, 1990, 2003 and 2015, and non-US police photos, are not covered by that line, and their status must be checked one by one. YouTube's own pages say nothing specific about mugshots.
findings.action: Keep a rights log per video: for each image, the source plus why you may use it (public domain with the reason, licence, or own illustration). Where status is unclear, especially news-agency photos and UK police images, use your own illustrations or silhouettes, as the first script already does.

findings.topic: Reused and inauthentic content: scans, slideshows and reading the record aloud
findings.official_quote: Content that exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create, like text from websites or news feeds ... Image slideshows, templated storylines, or scrolling text with minimal or no narrative, commentary, or educational value ... Our reused content policy applies to your channel as a whole.
findings.applies: A faceless channel whose visuals are newspaper scans, document pages, text cards and stills is exactly the format these YouTube Partner Program rules describe. 'Told from the record' must not become reading transcripts or articles aloud over scrolling pages. The first script is original narration with its own structure, so it passes. Reviewers also check 'Video metadata (including titles, thumbnails, and descriptions)' and the 'Channel’s “About” section'.
findings.action: Write original narration for every video. Quote records only in short excerpts that you then explain, and vary the visual treatment and story structure between cases. Use the About text to say how each episode is researched and written, so reviewers can see the work is yours.

findings.topic: AI reconstructions and voices of real people
findings.official_quote: Creators must disclose GenAI content that: • Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn’t do. • Alters footage of a real event or place. • Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. ... Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI
findings.applies: The script calls for illustrations, silhouettes and text cards. Those are non-realistic, so no disclosure is needed. If later videos use photorealistic AI reconstructions of real people (Peruggia, Lustig, Cooper) or real places, the 'AI use' answer at upload must be Yes. The Harassment policy separately bans 'Content that realistically simulates deceased or abused individuals describing their death or violence experienced', for example an AI voice of an injured guard or driver telling their ordeal.
findings.action: Keep the non-photorealistic illustration style. If any upload includes realistic AI imagery or voices of real people or events, answer Yes under 'AI use' in YouTube Studio. Never give an AI voice to a victim describing what was done to them.

findings.topic: Made for kids
findings.official_quote: General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”
findings.applies: Crime from court records is a teen and adult subject. The illustrated style does not make it child-directed, because YouTube lists 'Animated content that appeals to everyone' as general audience and says it is 'your legal responsibility to comply with COPPA'.
findings.action: Set the channel and every video to 'No, it's not made for kids', and don't use child-oriented characters, songs or keywords in metadata.

review.notes:
No kit wording conflicts with a YouTube rule, so I have no kit_edit. The description's promises ('No guessing about guilt, no graphic detail for its own sake, and respect for the real people involved') match the rules. They only protect a video when the narration itself carries that context, because YouTube does not count channel descriptions as EDSA context. Nothing in the ten titles or the Mona Lisa script breaks a policy. 'Next: how he got it out of the building' is fine as long as that episode stays a story and does not become a technique guide.

Minor, not listed as a finding: 'The Forger Who Fooled the Nazis' can show Nazi-era imagery. The advertiser-friendly guidelines put 'Educational or documentary content: ... Containing focal hate imagery.' under 'This content can earn ad revenue'. The Hate speech policy allows 'Historical footage of an event, like WWII, which doesn't promote violence or hatred' but requires that 'this context must appear in the images or audio of the video itself'. So narrate the context, and avoid a bare swastika as the thumbnail's main image.

YouTube's pages say nothing specific about mugshots. The rules that cover them are privacy, harassment (PII) and copyright, as above. Whether a particular mugshot, UK custody photo or press photo is public domain is a legal question YouTube leaves to the uploader; I did not answer it from memory.

How I read the pages: every quote comes from support.google.com through the reader. The reader drops repeated lines, which removes the ad-earning column labels on the Advertiser-friendly guidelines page. To confirm which column each quoted row sits in, I fetched that same official page once with curl and read the table structure. The quotes themselves are unchanged. The reader also showed an unrelated impersonation paragraph at the top of the violence and harassment pages; I ignored it. I wrote temporary text copies of pages in the scratchpad and deleted them, so no files are left. I did not touch the website repository.

proved.audience_setting: Not made for kids. YouTube's Help Center says: "General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9528076, confirmed). Historic crime told from court records is meant for teens and adults. The illustrated style doesn't change that, because YouTube lists "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as general audience. Set it for the whole channel and for each upload, and keep kid-targeted words and characters out of titles, tags and thumbnails. The age-restriction page also says "Your "made for kids" settings won't impact age restrictions on your videos."

kept.topic: Doxxing: addresses and phone numbers in court files, police reports and newspaper scans
kept.official_quote: Content that shares, threatens to share, or encourages others to share non-public personally identifiable information (PII). ... PII includes, but isn’t limited to, home addresses; email addresses; sign-in credentials, like a username or password; phone numbers; passport numbers; medical records; bank account information; or the name of a school a minor attends. ... This doesn't include posting widely available public information, like an official’s office phone number or the phone number of a business. ... This policy applies to sharing your own PII, sharing someone else’s PII, and situations where you accidentally share PII. (Harassment policy.) The EDSA page lists under 'Content that may not get EDSA exceptions': "Content that reveals an individual’s private information, such as their home address, email addresses, sign-in credentials, phone numbers, passport number, or bank account information (doxxing)"
kept.applies: The channel is built on court files, police reports, FBI files and newspapers, which often print home addresses, phone numbers and account details of defendants, witnesses, tipsters and victims. The risk is highest in recent cases where people may still be alive: Hatton Garden (2015), Antwerp (2003), the Gardner heist (1990) and the D. B. Cooper files, which name many tipsters and suspects. The policy covers accidental sharing too, so a number visible in a scanned page counts. YouTube's EDSA page (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/6345162) says doxxing 'may not' get an exception 'even if it has context added', so documentary framing may not save a video that shows an address. (Corrected: the review said framing 'does not' save it. YouTube's word is 'may not'.)
kept.action: Before any document or clipping goes on screen, blur home addresses, phone numbers, account and ID numbers, and any minor's school, especially for anyone who is or may be alive. YouTube's carve-out covers only 'widely available public information, like an official’s office phone number or the phone number of a business'. No YouTube rule requires blurring a century-old address, but doing it costs nothing.

kept.topic: Real people in mugshots and photos: privacy complaints, including from families of the dead
kept.official_quote: We also consider public interest, newsworthiness, consent, and whether the information is otherwise publicly available. ... A close family member makes the claim for a deceased individual. ... When a privacy complaint is filed, we may give the creator time to remove or edit the private info in their video. During this time, the creator can use the Trim or Blur tools in YouTube Studio to edit the video. ... If we remove your video for a privacy violation, do not upload another version featuring the same people. ... Incomplete methods of removal are not acceptable and include: Making a video private.
kept.applies: Mugshots, custody photos and newspaper portraits show people who are 'uniquely identifiable'. Some may still be alive, such as Hatton Garden gang members, members of the Antwerp ring and the Gardner Museum guards. Others are dead but have close family who can complain, such as Great Train Robbery defendants and the injured train driver. YouTube weighs 'public interest, newsworthiness, consent' and public availability, but doesn't say how much each counts. It's reasonable to expect that a convicted defendant's role in a famous case counts for more than a relative's, bystander's, juror's or never-charged person's. YouTube 'may' give the creator time to trim or blur; it doesn't promise to. (Corrected: the review stated who was alive as fact and implied there was always a deadline to act.)
kept.action: Show faces only of people central to the documented case: convicted people, and officials acting in their role. Blur or leave out relatives, bystanders, witnesses and never-charged suspects. If a privacy complaint arrives with time to act, trim or blur the person; making the video private doesn't count. Never re-upload a removed video with the same people.

kept.topic: Unsolved cases and suspects: defamation, and no ads for 'slander and defamation'
kept.official_quote: Malicious personal attacks, slander, and defamation. (Advertiser-friendly guidelines, under 'This content will receive no ad earnings'.) Defamation page (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/6154230): "We take into account local legal considerations in our defamation blocking process, and in some cases, we require a court order." ... "Consistent with Section 230(c) of the Communications Decency Act, we recommend that you pursue any claims you may have directly against the person who posted the content."
kept.applies: 'D. B. Cooper: What the Files Actually Say' and 'The Gardner Museum Heist' are unsolved. The FBI files name people who were never charged, and some of them or their families may be alive. Hatton Garden, the Great Train Robbery and Piltdown are British stories, and YouTube applies 'local legal considerations' when blocking for defamation. YouTube's US defamation page sends people with defamation claims to the uploader, not to YouTube, so the legal risk falls on the creator personally. (The defamation quotes are on 6154230, not the source_url above.) The kit's 'No guessing about guilt' is the right protection, and the Mona Lisa script already follows it ('Neither had anything to do with it').
kept.action: In unsolved cases, describe named people only as the record does ('the FBI investigated X; X was never charged'), with the source on screen. Never say or suggest guilt beyond a conviction. Keep an uncharged person's face and name out of titles and thumbnails.

kept.topic: Crime documentaries can earn ads; how-to detail, glorifying theft and bare CCTV earn none
kept.official_quote: Documentaries about crime. (under 'This content can earn ad revenue') ... Content meant to educate viewers on how to gain unauthorized access or make unauthorized changes to systems, devices, or property in malicious ways. ... Displaying a house break-in without additional context, e.g. CCTV footage of a house break-in. (under 'This content will receive no ad earnings'). The section is headed 'Enabling dishonest behavior: Content glorifying or promoting dishonest behavior, such as trespassing, cheating, or computer hacking that is personal or paid for.'
kept.applies: Six of the ten titles are heists or thefts. The Mona Lisa script ends 'Next: how he got it out of the building.' Hatton Garden (drilling into a vault) and Antwerp (getting past vault security) invite technical walk-throughs, and police released CCTV of the Hatton Garden gang. A history told as a story is in the ad-earning column. A how-to method or CCTV without context is in the no-ads column. (The CCTV example is about a house break-in, the closest example YouTube gives.) The Community Guidelines also ban 'Instructional theft videos posted with the express intent to steal physical goods or get something for free' (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2801964) and 'Footage of crimes such as violent robberies that provide no education or explanation to viewers' (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2802008). I confirmed the column of each quoted row in the page's own table structure.
kept.action: Tell the method at story level: what happened, why it worked in that year, and how the thieves were caught. Leave out reusable specifics such as tool models, alarm-defeat steps and vault layouts. Always narrate over CCTV or police footage. Don't present the theft as something to admire or copy. (Corrected: YouTube bans no particular words such as 'genius'; the rule is about glorifying or promoting.)

kept.topic: Violence, injuries and crime-scene images: ad limits, and context must be in the video
kept.official_quote: Content where the focal point is on blood, violence, or injury, when presented without other context, is not suitable for advertising. ... A documentary on a recent homicide featuring descriptive language of the circumstances of death. (limited ad earnings) ... Focus on blood, guts, gore, bodily fluids (human or animal), crime scenes or accident photos with little to no context. (no ad earnings). Violent or graphic content policy: "For educational content containing the kinds of violent or graphic content noted above, this context must appear in the images or audio of the video itself. Providing it in the title or description is insufficient."
kept.applies: Most of the ten titles involve little violence. The exceptions are the Great Train Robbery, where the driver was struck and injured; D. B. Cooper, an air hijacking; and the description's word 'disappearances'. The EDSA page says 'We may not make EDSA exceptions for context that may be in comments, tags, channel descriptions, pinned comments, or other surfaces.' The violent extremist or criminal organizations policy (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9229472) adds: 'If posting content related to terrorism or crime for an educational, documentary, scientific, or artistic purpose, be mindful to provide enough information in the video or audio itself so viewers understand the context.' So the channel description's promise of 'no graphic detail for its own sake' doesn't count as context for any single video; each video's narration has to carry it. (Corrected: the review said the promise 'protects nothing'. It only matters for a video that needs an exception.) The Harassment policy also bans 'Content reveling in or mocking the death or serious injury of an identifiable individual.'
kept.action: Describe injuries and deaths briefly, without graphic detail. Keep crime-scene, injury and body photos out of thumbnails and off screen. Say the who, when, where and why aloud in the narration, and never treat a victim's injury as part of the fun of a heist.

kept.topic: Mugshots, newspaper scans and archive photos: copyright; a credit is not a licence
kept.official_quote: Ultimately, it's your responsibility to verify that a work is in the public domain before you upload it to YouTube. ... For example, works created by U.S. government agencies are automatically in the public domain. ... Rules vary by country/region, but generally copyright lasts for the life of the author plus 50-70 years. (Copyright on YouTube.) Common copyright myths (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2797449): "Giving credit to the copyright owner doesn’t automatically give you the rights to use their copyrighted content."
kept.applies: The description promises 'Sources are listed under every video'. That builds trust, but YouTube says credit doesn't give rights, and its dispute page (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2797454) lists 'Giving credit to the copyright owner' among reasons that are 'NOT legitimate reasons to dispute a claim'. Material the FBI itself created fits YouTube's 'U.S. government agencies' example. (Corrected: the review said all FBI material does. A newspaper clipping or private photo kept in an FBI file wasn't created by the agency, so it isn't covered.) Because copyright 'generally' runs for 'the life of the author plus 50-70 years', even 1911–1914 press photos aren't automatically free. Press and agency images from 1963, 1990, 2003 and 2015, and non-US police photos, must be checked one by one. The myths page adds that for fair use or public domain, 'only a court of law can make that determination'. YouTube's pages say nothing specific about mugshots.
kept.action: Keep a rights log for each video: for every image, the source and why you may use it (public domain and the reason, a licence, or your own illustration). Where the status is unclear, especially news-agency photos and UK police images, use your own illustrations or silhouettes, as the first script already does.

kept.topic: Reused and inauthentic content: scans, slideshows and reading the record aloud
kept.official_quote: Content that exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create, like text from websites or news feeds ... Image slideshows, templated storylines, or scrolling text with minimal or no narrative, commentary, or educational value ... Our reused content policy applies to your channel as a whole. If you have videos that violate our guidelines, or if we cannot clearly tell that you made the content, monetization may be removed from your entire channel.
kept.applies: A faceless channel built on newspaper scans, document pages, text cards and stills is exactly the format these YouTube Partner Program rules describe. 'Told from the record' must not turn into reading transcripts or articles aloud over scrolling pages. The page also says the policy 'applies even if you have permission from the original creator' and is 'not based on copyright, permission, or fair use', so public-domain scans can still count as reused content. The first script is the kind of original, structured narration the policy rewards, though YouTube judges the channel as a whole, not one script. (Corrected: the review said the script 'passes'.) Reviewers may check 'Video metadata (including titles, thumbnails, and descriptions)' and the 'Channel’s “About” section'.
kept.action: Write original narration for every video. Quote records in short excerpts that you then explain, and vary the visuals and story structure between cases. Use the About text to say how each episode is researched and written, so reviewers can see the work is yours.

kept.topic: AI reconstructions and voices of real people
kept.official_quote: Creators must disclose GenAI content that: • Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn’t do. • Alters footage of a real event or place. • Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. ... Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI ... Examples of content, edits, or video assistance that creators need to disclose: ... Depicting a public figure stealing something they did not steal, or admitting to stealing something when they did not make that admission • Making it look like a real person has been arrested or imprisoned
kept.applies: The script calls for illustrations, silhouettes and text cards. Those aren't realistic, so no disclosure is needed. If later videos use photorealistic AI reconstructions of real people (Peruggia, Lustig, Cooper) or real places, the 'AI use' answer at upload must be Yes. YouTube's own examples (arrests, imprisonment, theft) are this channel's subject matter. Separately, when someone complains about an AI likeness, the privacy page (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/7671399) says YouTube considers whether 'The content features a public figure or well-known individual engaging in a sensitive behavior, such as criminal activity, violence'. The Harassment policy bans 'Content that realistically simulates deceased or abused individuals describing their death or violence experienced'. The page also says creators who 'consistently choose not to disclose' may face 'removal of content or suspension from the YouTube Partner Program'.
kept.action: Keep the non-photorealistic illustration style. If any upload includes realistic AI imagery or voices of real people or real events, answer Yes under 'AI use' in YouTube Studio. Never give an AI voice to a victim describing what was done to them.

kept.topic: Made for kids
kept.official_quote: General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”
kept.applies: Crime from court records is a teen and adult subject. The illustrated style doesn't make it child-directed: YouTube lists 'Animated content that appeals to everyone' as general audience and says 'it is your legal responsibility to comply with COPPA and/or other applicable laws and designate your content accurately.'
kept.action: Set the channel and every video to 'No, it's not made for kids', and keep child-oriented characters, songs and keywords out of metadata.

added.topic: Thumbnails: no gore, no shock, no misleading 'reveal'
added.official_quote: Don’t post a thumbnail or other image on YouTube if it shows: ... • Violent imagery that intends to shock or disgust • Graphic or disturbing imagery with blood or gore ... • A thumbnail that misleads viewers to think they’re about to view something that’s not in the video ... Sometimes, a thumbnail may not be appropriate for all audiences, but it doesn’t violate our Community Guidelines. When that happens, we may age-restrict the video, or we may remove the thumbnail, but we don’t issue a strike on your channel. ... If your thumbnail violates other policies, we remove the thumbnail and may issue a strike against your account.
added.applies: True-crime thumbnails are usually where channels get into trouble: crime-scene photos, bloodied faces, or a 'suspect revealed' face for a case that was never solved. 'D. B. Cooper: What the Files Actually Say' and the Gardner heist are both unsolved. A thumbnail suggesting the case is solved, or showing a named suspect as the culprit, risks the 'misleads viewers' rule as well as defamation. YouTube judges 'Whether violent or gory imagery is the focal point of the thumbnail' and 'Whether the title, description, tags, or other data indicate an intent to shock or disgust viewers.' The policy covers 'banners, avatars, posts' too.
added.action: Build thumbnails from the channel's own illustrations: the object, the place or a silhouette. Use no blood, injuries or crime-scene photos. Show only what the video actually shows and says, and never present an unsolved case as solved or an uncharged person as guilty.

added.topic: Age restriction: crime documentaries can be limited to signed-in adults, with fewer ads
added.official_quote: We may apply an age restriction or warning to content even if it gets an EDSA exception because it may not be appropriate for viewers under 18 (e.g. violent crime footage in a documentary). (EDSA page, https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/6345162.) Age-restricted content page: "Age-restricted videos are not viewable to users who are under 18 years of age or signed out." ... "Age-restricted videos can use ads to monetize. Some advertisers prefer to advertise on family-friendly content or content without the themes noted above. In this case, your video may have limited or no ads monetization."
added.applies: YouTube names 'violent crime footage in a documentary' as its example of content that can be allowed and still be age-restricted. An age-restricted video loses signed-out and under-18 viewers, can't be watched on most other websites, and 'may have limited or no ads monetization'. Most of this channel's cases are non-violent, so the risk sits in the few violent ones (the Great Train Robbery assault) and in any real footage or photos of injuries. Page examples include 'A video with context showing survivor's injuries in a major road accident'.
added.action: Tell violent moments in narration and illustration, not with real footage or photos of injuries. After each upload, check YouTube Studio's Content page for 'Viewable by 18+' under Notices, and appeal if it was applied by mistake.

added.topic: Unsolved cases: don't send viewers after real people
added.official_quote: Content that encourages abusive behavior, like brigading. Brigading is when an individual encourages the coordinated abuse of an identifiable individual on or off YouTube. ... Content that contains stalking of an identifiable individual. ... This policy applies to videos, video descriptions, comments, live streams, and any other YouTube product or feature.
added.applies: The review covered doxxing and defamation, but not what an unsolved-case channel invites its audience to do. D. B. Cooper and the Gardner heist attract amateur sleuths, and the FBI files name tipsters, suspects and their families, some of whom may be alive. A video or pinned comment asking viewers to 'help solve it' by digging into, contacting or watching named people could be read as encouraging abuse or stalking of an identifiable individual. Among the rare cases where the harassment page says YouTube 'may remove content or issue other penalties' is when a creator 'Repeatedly encourages abusive audience behavior.' Pointing viewers to the official tip lines is a different thing from this.
added.action: Never ask viewers to investigate, find, contact or watch a named living person or their family. If you mention tips, point only to the official FBI or museum channels. In comments, remove anything that posts a named person's details or urges people to go after them.

proved.notes:
Every quote in the review was found word for word on the official page it names, or on a related YouTube Help page that I now cite in the finding. Nothing was invented, so nothing was struck. My corrections are about overstatement: 'may not' instead of 'does not' for EDSA doxxing exceptions; YouTube 'may' give time to blur after a privacy complaint; FBI-created material is public domain, but clippings or private photos inside FBI files aren't; YouTube bans glorifying theft, not words like 'genius'; one script can't 'pass' a channel-wide policy; who is still alive is stated as 'may be'. Two quotes had the wrong page attached: the defamation-page lines are on https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/6154230, and the credit myth is on https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2797449. Both are now named in the findings.

Checking the columns: the reader drops repeated labels on the Advertiser-friendly guidelines page. So I fetched that same official page with curl and printed its text without deduplication, piped straight to stdout. This confirmed: 'Documentaries about crime' is under 'can earn ad revenue'; the unauthorized-access and house break-in rows are under 'no ad earnings'; 'A documentary on a recent homicide...' is under 'limited ad earnings'; 'Focus on blood, guts, gore...' is under 'no ad earnings'; 'Malicious personal attacks, slander, and defamation.' is under 'no ad earnings'; 'Educational or documentary content: ... Containing focal hate imagery.' is under 'can earn ad revenue'.

The review's note on 'The Forger Who Fooled the Nazis' checks out. The Hate speech policy (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2801939) allows 'Historical footage of an event, like WWII, which doesn't promote violence or hatred' and says 'this context must appear in the images or audio of the video itself.' Narrate the context, and don't make a bare swastika the main image of a thumbnail.

No kit wording conflicts with a YouTube rule, so I propose no kit_edit. The description's three promises match the rules. The Mona Lisa script's handling of Apollinaire and Picasso ('Both were let go. Neither had anything to do with it.') is a good model for the habit on unsolved cases.

Housekeeping: I briefly wrote one text copy of the ad guidelines page into the scratchpad (afg.txt) and deleted it straight away. No other files were written, and I didn't touch the website repository or git.

review.audience_setting: Not made for kids: the videos explain deductibles, escrow, leases, liens and contracts for adults, and YouTube's page says "General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”" The simple animated visuals don't change this, because the page also says a video is "not necessarily made for kids just because" it is "safe or appropriate for everyone to watch" and lists "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as general audience.

findings.topic: AI personas on sensitive topics (legal, finance)
findings.official_quote: This policy refers to channels that use AI-generated personas to deliver information on sensitive topics. This includes any content that presents itself as a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances, or politics. To protect viewers who may be confused or otherwise negatively impacted by this content, channels uploading this content will not be allowed to monetize. [examples include] AI-generated podcast hosts offering financial guidance, investment tips, or wealth management advice / AI personas giving legal advice or interpreting laws
findings.applies: Every topic on this channel is a legal or money topic under this policy: contracts, leases, liens, insurance and closings. Titles such as "What 'As Is' Means in a Contract" and "How to Read a Lease" interpret legal documents, which is the policy's own example ("interpreting laws"). The kit as written is fine: there is no host, only animated bills, bars and a narrator. The risk is what a faceless channel often adds later, such as an AI presenter, an AI "attorney", "agent" or "broker" character, or two AI podcast hosts. Any of those would make the whole channel ineligible to earn money. This is the one rule that could end monetization for the entire channel, not just one video.
findings.action: Keep the narrator a plain voice, ideally the owner's own voice or a clone of it. Never use an on-screen AI presenter, a named AI character, or an AI host who talks as if they are a lawyer, agent, broker or adviser, and never write lines like "as an attorney" or "in my years as an agent".

findings.topic: Inauthentic (templated) content
findings.official_quote: Generic or repetitive content includes content that looks like it’s made with a template, or that may feel repetitive to viewers after watching several videos in a row from the same channel. ... What’s important is that the substance of each video should be materially varied and deliver creative, educational, or other value.
findings.applies: The kit sets up a fixed format: "Each video explains one term or one document with a simple worked example." The first script uses one sequence of visuals: a bill, two split bars, a seesaw, a calendar, a three-question checklist and a closing title card. The page allows a series ("Same intro and outro for your videos, but the bulk of your content is different"). It refuses "AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective". Reviewers check the "Main theme", "Newest videos" and the "Channel’s ‘About’ section". So ten videos that all run bill, bars, seesaw, checklist would look interchangeable.
findings.action: Keep only the short open and the closing card the same. Give each video its own worked example and its own visuals: a lease page for leases, a closing table timeline for closings, a lien on a property record for liens. Don't reuse the "three questions to ask" checklist as a fixed segment.

findings.topic: Mass-produced AI videos (Spam policy)
findings.official_quote: Automated or synthetic mass-production: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don't allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content.
findings.applies: This is a Community Guidelines rule, not just a monetization rule. The page says it can lead to warnings, strikes, suspended monetization or a terminated channel. Its example describes the typical faceless explainer setup: "Channels that use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos, with each video reading out an AI-generated script." A glossary channel can produce hundreds of near-identical term videos, which makes it unusually exposed to this rule.
findings.action: Publish at a pace where each script is researched and checked by a person. Vary the music and imagery between videos, and don't batch-generate dozens of term videos from one prompt.

findings.topic: AI disclosure setting ("AI use")
findings.official_quote: Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI, or edits to realistic content that are minor.
findings.applies: The kit's animated bills, bars and seesaw are non-realistic, so they need no disclosure. Narration cloned from the owner's own voice is on the Help page's list of things that need no disclosure ("Cloning one’s own voice to create voice overs or dubs"). A stock AI voice that sounds like a real person is not on either list of the current Help page. However, YouTube's March 18, 2024 blog post (https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/disclosing-ai-generated-content) listed "synthetically generating a person’s voice to narrate a video" as needing disclosure. The same post said "for videos that touch on more sensitive topics — like health, news, elections, or finance — we’ll also show a more prominent label on the video itself." That post is from 2024, and the current Help page describes labels differently. The Help page also says: "Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money."
findings.action: At upload, under Attributes > "AI use": answer No for animated graphics narrated by the owner or the owner's own voice clone. Answer Yes if the narration is a stock AI voice or if any realistic AI imagery is used, such as a photoreal house, office or person.

findings.topic: Sponsorships and affiliate deals in financial services
findings.official_quote: Some categories of branded content come with additional restrictions. To promote goods, services, or brands in these categories, you are responsible for confirming that your brand partners are certified by Google as necessary. You are also responsible to comply with all applicable legal requirements–including using age and country restrictions.
findings.applies: "Financial Services" is on that page's list of restricted categories. This niche will attract offers from mortgage lenders, loan, credit-repair and debt companies, insurers, quote-comparison sites and legal-document services. Google Ads defines financial services as "products and services related to the management or investment of money and cryptocurrencies, including personalized advice" (https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/2464998), and some countries require advertisers to pass "location-specific financial services verification". The branded content page also says any deal "in exchange for payment, free products, or sponsorships (whether you receive the benefit now or later on)" counts, so affiliate commissions very likely count too. A violation "applies to the entirety of your content, not just the portion where the branded content or sponsorship appears."
findings.action: For every sponsored or affiliate video, tick "My video contains paid promotion" in Studio. Before accepting any lender, credit, debt, insurance or investment partner, ask them for proof they are certified or verified by Google for the countries the video reaches, and use the age and country limits that box offers when required.

findings.topic: Quality signals for trust topics (what blogs call YMYL)
findings.official_quote: For quality, our systems are designed to identify signals that can help determine which channels demonstrate expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness on a given topic.
findings.applies: YouTube's own pages never say "YMYL". That label comes from Google Search's rater guidelines, which the reader can't open, so treat "YMYL" as unofficial on YouTube. What YouTube does say is that search weighs expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness for every topic. It names extra steps only for "news, politics, medical, and scientific info", not law or finance. It also says evaluators "look at factors like the expertise and reputation of the speaker or channel, the main topic of the video, and whether the content delivers on its promise or achieves its goal." A faceless channel on money and contracts has to earn those signals through accuracy and sourcing, because it can't rely on a credentialed face.
findings.action: Put each video's sources in its description, such as the state insurance department, CFPB or HUD pages or the relevant statute, and pin a correction when something is wrong. Make every title deliver exactly what it promises.

findings.topic: "Required" disclaimers
findings.applies: Only third-party "faceless channel" guides say finance or legal channels must carry a "not advice" disclaimer. None of the YouTube pages read (monetization policies, Spam policy, branded content, AI disclosure, impersonation) requires one, and none says a disclaimer protects a video. The kit already has a good one in the description ("This channel is general education only. It is not legal, insurance or financial advice...") and a spoken one at the end of the script. That fits the AI-persona rule, which targets content that "presents itself as a human expert providing advice". Laws outside YouTube, such as the FTC's sponsorship rules, are separate, and the branded content page says "You and the partners you work with are also responsible for understanding and complying with all applicable legal requirements."
findings.action: Keep the existing disclaimer lines as they are; no change needed. Don't treat them as a shield: what keeps the channel safe is never having a persona that gives advice and never presenting sponsored products as recommendations.

findings.topic: Made for kids
findings.official_quote: General audience content is content that could appeal to everyone, but isn’t intended specifically for children, or content that is intended for a teen or older audience. General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”
findings.applies: The subjects (deductibles, escrow, leases, liens, closings, life insurance) are for adults. review.notes:
The kit's wording doesn't conflict with any official rule I read, so I have no kit_edit. kept.topic: AI personas on sensitive topics (legal, finance)
kept.official_quote: This policy refers to channels that use AI-generated personas to deliver information on sensitive topics. This includes any content that presents itself as a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances, or politics. To protect viewers who may be confused or otherwise negatively impacted by this content, channels uploading this content will not be allowed to monetize. ... • AI-generated podcast hosts offering financial guidance, investment tips, or wealth management advice • AI personas giving legal advice or interpreting laws
kept.applies: Every subject on this channel (contracts, leases, liens, insurance, closings) is legal or money, which the policy names as sensitive. Explaining what a lease or an "as is" clause says is close to the policy's example "interpreting laws", but the policy only bites when an AI persona does it while presenting "itself as a human expert providing advice". The kit as written is fine: no host, only animated bills, bars and a narrator who calls the videos "general education". The risk is what faceless channels often add later: an AI presenter, an AI "attorney", "agent" or "broker" character, or two AI podcast hosts. The penalty is for the whole channel ("channels uploading this content will not be allowed to monetize"), not one video. (Correction: the review called this "the one rule" that could end monetization for the whole channel. That's not right, because the inauthentic-content and reused-content rules also apply to the whole channel. It also marked this a blocker, but nothing in the kit breaks it.)
kept.action: Keep the narrator a plain voice, ideally your own voice or a clone of your own voice. Never use an on-screen AI presenter, a named AI character, or AI hosts who speak as a lawyer, agent, broker or adviser, and never script lines like "as an attorney" or "in my years as an agent".

kept.topic: Inauthentic (templated) content
kept.official_quote: Generic or repetitive content includes content that looks like it’s made with a template, or that may feel repetitive to viewers after watching several videos in a row from the same channel. ... What’s important is that the substance of each video should be materially varied and deliver creative, educational, or other value.
kept.applies: The kit sets a fixed format: "Each video explains one term or one document with a simple worked example." The first script runs one sequence: bill, two split bars, seesaw, calendar, a three-question checklist, title card. A series format is allowed. The page says "We know many channels create content that follows a similar pattern", and lists "Same intro and outro for your videos, but the bulk of your content is different" as allowed. What it refuses is "AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective". It applies to the channel as a whole: "channels where content feels interchangeable from video to video are not allowed to monetize." Reviewers "may focus on" (the review said "check") the channel's "Main theme", "Newest videos", "Video metadata (including titles, thumbnails, and descriptions)" and "Channel’s “About” section". Ten videos that all run bill, bars, seesaw, checklist with only the numbers changed would risk looking interchangeable.
kept.action: Keep the open and the closing card the same if you like. Give each video its own worked example and visuals that suit the subject: a lease page for leases, a closing-day timeline for closings, a lien on a property record for liens. A recurring "questions to ask" segment is fine if its questions are specific to each topic; don't paste the same three questions into every video. (Correction: the review said to drop the checklist as a fixed segment, but the policy allows a repeated pattern when the substance varies.)

kept.topic: Mass-produced AI videos (Spam policy)
kept.official_quote: Automated or synthetic mass-production: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don't allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content.
kept.applies: This is a platform rule, not only a monetization rule. The page says "we may suspend your monetization or terminate your channel or account" and "For some violations, we may remove the content and issue a warning or a strike against your channel." Its example matches a common faceless-explainer setup: "Channels that use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos, with each video reading out an AI-generated script." A glossary channel could produce hundreds of near-identical term videos, which makes it more exposed than most.
kept.action: Publish at a pace where a person researches and checks each script. Vary the music and imagery between videos, and don't batch-generate dozens of term videos from one prompt.

kept.topic: AI disclosure setting ("AI use")
kept.official_quote: Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI, or edits to realistic content that are minor.
kept.applies: The kit's animated bills, bars and seesaw are not realistic, so they need no disclosure. The page's no-disclosure examples include "Using an AI-generated or altered animation of a missile in a fully animated video". Narration in your own cloned voice is on the no-disclosure list ("Cloning one’s own voice to create voice overs or dubs"). A lifelike stock AI voice is on neither list. The must-disclose list is about realistic content, such as "Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn’t do" and "Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur". YouTube's March 18, 2024 blog post (https://blog.youtube/news-and-events/disclosing-ai-generated-content) put "synthetically generating a person’s voice to narrate a video" under "Using the likeness of a realistic person". So a stock voice is a grey area, not a stated requirement. (Correction: the review presented that blog line as a plain rule for any synthetic narrator.) The Spam policy also says "Creators should disclose when content is generated or meaningfully altered with AI, but this disclosure is not a free pass to violate our policies." The review missed AI music: the Help page says creators must disclose GenAI content that "Creates music that’s the main focus of the video", and it lists "AI generated music" among the examples that need disclosure. The 2024 blog promised "a more prominent label on the video itself" for finance topics. The current page instead says a player label "may also appear" "For AI-generated music or content that is photorealistic", so the topic-based label may be out of date. The page also says "Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money."
kept.action: At upload, under Attributes > "AI use": answer No for animated graphics narrated in your own voice or your own voice clone. Answer Yes if any realistic AI imagery is used (a photoreal house, office or person) or if the music is AI-generated. If you use a lifelike stock AI voice, Yes isn't clearly required, but it is the safe choice and costs nothing in reach or earnings. Using YouTube Audio Library or other licensed music avoids the AI music question.

kept.topic: Sponsorships and affiliate deals in financial services
kept.official_quote: Some categories of branded content come with additional restrictions. To promote goods, services, or brands in these categories, you are responsible for confirming that your brand partners are certified by Google as necessary. You are also responsible to comply with all applicable legal requirements–including using age and country restrictions.
kept.applies: "Financial Services" is on that page's list of restricted categories, and this niche will attract lenders, credit, debt, insurance and investment sponsors. Google Ads defines financial services as "products and services related to the management or investment of money and cryptocurrencies, including personalized advice", and says "You’re required to complete a verification process to advertise financial services in some locations." (https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/2464998). Google's list of categories that may need that verification includes "Credit and loans", "Investment" and "Insurance" (https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/15332319). The review missed that the same Ads page says "Ads for credit repair services are not allowed." It also allows debt services only "in select locations". The branded content page says branded content "must comply with YouTube’s Community Guidelines and Google Ads policies , with some exceptions where those policies may not be applicable to branded content", so credit-repair sponsors are very likely off-limits. Legal-document services don't fit Google's definition of financial services. The page doesn't name affiliate links. It covers content "influenced by a brand partner in exchange for something of value", including payment "(whether you receive the benefit now or later on)", so a partner deal that pays commission is safest treated as branded content. (Correction: the review said affiliates "very likely count"; the page doesn't say so.) A violation "applies to the entirety of your content, not just the portion where the branded content or sponsorship appears."
kept.action: For every sponsored video, and every video where a partner pays you for links, tick "My video contains paid promotion" in Studio. Turn down credit-repair sponsors. Before accepting a lender, credit-card, debt, insurance or investment partner, ask for proof that they hold Google's financial services verification where Google requires it, and use the box's age and country limits when the law requires them.

added.topic: Reused content (reading out official definitions)
added.official_quote: Content that exclusively features readings of other materials you did not originally create, like text from websites or news feeds
added.applies: That line is on the page's list of reused content that's not allowed to monetize. A glossary channel is drawn to read definitions straight from CFPB, HUD, state insurance department or insurer pages, especially once the quality finding tells the owner to source each video from them. Reading those aloud, or showing them as scrolling text, is the pattern this policy describes. The inauthentic-content section on the same page also refuses "Image slideshows, templated storylines, or scrolling text with minimal or no narrative, commentary, or educational value". The penalty can reach the whole channel: "Our reused content policy applies to your channel as a whole. If you have videos that violate our guidelines, or if we cannot clearly tell that you made the content, monetization may be removed from your entire channel." The first script is written in the owner's own words with a made-up example, which is what the policy rewards.

The review missed AI music: "Creates music that’s the main focus of the video" must be disclosed, and "AI generated music" is on the list of examples that need disclosure.

Insurance is confirmed as a category that can need Google's financial services verification (https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/15332319). Legal-document services are not financial services.
