Added: reused content, because reading official definitions aloud is a real risk for a glossary channel and its penalty is channel-wide.

Confirmed from the reviewer's notes: the impersonation policy bars "Using a channel name or handle that is phonetically identical or visually similar to an established entity. This includes the use of deceptive misspellings." It also says impersonation "may include deceptively copying the branding, content, or usernames of individuals, channels or entities", which supports the advice not to use a real insurer's or agency's logo. The deductible note is a fact-check point, not a YouTube rule. It holds: the $400 "insurer pays nothing ... no point in claiming" line fits the car or home example, so keep it clearly about those, since the script then turns to health plans.

Not read: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines (the host can't be opened), so "YMYL" stays unconfirmed for YouTube. No kit_edit is needed; the kit's wording conflicts with no official rule I read. Pages read for this check: support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392, 2801973, 14328491, 17596007, 9528076, 9527654, 9962575, 2801947, 6162278; blog.youtube/news-and-events/disclosing-ai-generated-content; support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/2464998, 15332319, 15332527.

findings.topic: Generic or repetitive content (the renamed "inauthentic content" rule)
findings.official_quote: What’s important is that the substance of each video should be materially varied and deliver creative, educational, or other value. ... That means channels where content feels interchangeable from video to video are not allowed to monetize. ... Examples of what’s not allowed to monetize (this list is not exhaustive): • Similar or repetitive content with low educational value, commentary, narratives, or minimal variation across videos
findings.applies: Hours-long rain with no voice and a still picture is about as exposed to this rule as a channel can be: the sound is the only thing that can make one video different from the next. The ten titles are different sounds, which is good. But recipe step 5 says to publish every sound twice, as a 3-hour and an 8-hour cut. That makes half the catalogue near-copies of the other half, and that is exactly the "minimal variation across videos" YouTube names. The same page says reviewers focus on a channel's "Main theme", "Most viewed videos", "Newest videos" and "Biggest proportion of watch time". On a channel of 8-hour videos, a few long uploads will hold most of the watch time, so those must be the most clearly original ones. No official page names ambient, sleep or still-image videos as allowed or banned. The test is only whether each video is materially different.
findings.action: Give each sound one length, and make every upload a different recording or mix with its own place, layers and picture. Don't re-upload the same mix at a second length.

kit_edit.quote: 5. Length. Publish one 3-hour and one 8-hour version of each sound.
kit_edit.replace_with: 5. Length. Give each sound one length (3, 8 or 10 hours; YouTube's upload limit is 12). Don't upload the same mix again at another length: two videos of the same sound are interchangeable, and YouTube doesn't monetize channels where videos feel interchangeable.

findings.topic: Reused content: a licence or permission doesn't make it yours
findings.official_quote: Taking someone else’s content, making minimal changes, and calling it your own original work would be a violation of this guideline. If we cannot tell that the content is yours, it may be subject to our reused content policy. This policy applies even if you have permission from the original creator. ... • Content uploaded many times by other creators
findings.applies: Recipe step 1 says that sound "with a licence that allows commercial use on YouTube" is enough. That settles copyright, not YouTube's reused-content rule, which the same page says "is not based on copyright, permission, or fair use." Stock and library rain, including YouTube's own Audio Library effects, is used by many other channels. A video that is mostly one library rain track looped for hours is "Content uploaded many times by other creators", even when licensed.
findings.action: Record the main sound of every video yourself. Use a licensed sound only as one layer in your own mix, never as the whole video, and keep the licence.

kit_edit.quote: 1. Sound. Use rain you record yourself, or sound with a licence that allows commercial use on YouTube. Keep the licence. Sound copied from another channel is what gets these channels demonetized.
kit_edit.replace_with: 1. Sound. Record the main sound of every video yourself. A licensed sound can be one layer in your own mix, never the whole video: a licence settles copyright, but YouTube's reused-content rule applies even with permission, and the same library rain is on many other channels. Keep every licence. Never use sound copied from another channel.

findings.topic: Reused content is judged for the whole channel: show that you made it
findings.official_quote: Our reused content policy applies to your channel as a whole. If you have videos that violate our guidelines, or if we cannot clearly tell that you made the content, monetization may be removed from your entire channel.
findings.applies: With no face and no voice, a reviewer can't see or hear who made the recording. The page says reviewers check the "Channel description", "Video title" and "Video descriptions". It also allows "Reused content from other online sources where the creator is either visible in the content or explains how the creator added to the content". The description is where this channel shows it made the work. Recipe step 7 asks only for the sounds and the loop length, not how they were made.
findings.action: In every video description, say where and how the sound was recorded, what is layered in it and how long the loop is, and credit any licensed layer.

kit_edit.quote: 7. Description. Say what the sounds are and how long the loop is. Don't claim it treats insomnia, anxiety or any condition.
kit_edit.replace_with: 7. Description. Say what the sounds are, where and how you recorded them, what you layered together and how long the loop is, and credit any licensed sound. YouTube's reviewers read descriptions to tell whether you made the content. Don't claim it treats insomnia, anxiety or any condition.

findings.topic: Music and sound licensing: only the Audio Library is known to be copyright-safe
findings.official_quote: Only music and sound effects from the Audio Library are known to YouTube to be copyright-safe. • YouTube is not responsible for issues that arise from “royalty-free” music and sound effects from YouTube channels or other music libraries. ... If you’re using a track with a Creative Commons license, you must credit the artist in your video’s description.
findings.applies: The kit's titles include "Slow Piano and Light Rain for Studying" and the About text lists "a slow piano". Any piano or sound layer that isn't the owner's own recording comes from a library, and YouTube takes no responsibility for claims on "royalty-free" libraries outside the Audio Library. The About text currently says "All sound here is recorded or made for this channel." That stops being true as soon as a licensed layer is used. Also, the same page's reused-content rules bar "Collections of songs from different artists (even if you have their permission)", so the piano can't be a playlist of library tracks.
findings.action: Play or compose the piano yourself, or use one licensed track as a layer. Prefer the YouTube Audio Library for any outside sound, and credit Creative Commons tracks in the description. Make the About text say only what is true.

kit_edit.quote: All sound here is recorded or made for this channel.
kit_edit.replace_with: All sound here is recorded or mixed for this channel. Each video's description says where it was recorded, what is layered in it, and credits any licensed sound.

findings.topic: Phone verification and the 12-hour limit for long uploads
findings.official_quote: By default, you can upload videos that are up to 15 minutes long. Verified accounts can upload videos longer than 15 minutes. ... The maximum file size you can upload is 256 GB or 12 hours, whichever is less. ... If you could previously upload long videos and no longer can, check your account for copyright claims and strikes.
findings.applies: Every planned video is 2 to 10 hours long, so nothing can be uploaded until the account is verified. Longer "12 hours plus" uploads aren't possible. Because the whole channel depends on long uploads, a copyright strike, for example from unlicensed sound, threatens this channel more than most.
findings.action: Verify the account by phone before the first upload, and check that Feature eligibility shows long uploads as enabled. Keep every video under 12 hours, and treat any copyright claim or strike as urgent.

findings.topic: Mid-roll ads on sleep videos
findings.official_quote: By default, automatic mid-roll ad slots are selected for your video. ... While YouTube can automatically suggest the best placement for mid-roll ads, you may want to turn off mid-roll ads if not appropriate. For example, meditation videos may not be suitable for mid-roll ads.
findings.applies: The channel promises "no sudden noises ... so nothing pulls you back". Ads placed automatically through an 8-hour sleep video break that promise, and YouTube itself names meditation videos as a case where mid-rolls may not suit.
findings.action: Once monetized, choose deliberately. Either turn mid-rolls off for sleep videos and keep pre-roll only, or place a few manual slots and switch off automatic slots. Don't leave the default on without deciding.

findings.topic: Content ID can't protect rain and ambient recordings
findings.official_quote: You must have exclusive rights to the material in the reference file for the territories where you claim ownership. The following examples are ineligible for use in or as a reference: • Content licensed non-exclusively from a third party • Content released under Creative Commons or similar free of charge/open licenses ... • Sound effects, soundbeds, or production loops
findings.applies: The channel can't register its rain, wind or noise beds in Content ID, even through a distributor, and licensed or Creative Commons layers can never be registered. Re-uploads by other channels won't be caught automatically. The same rule also means nobody else may properly use a generic soundbed as a Content ID reference.
findings.action: Don't pay a distributor that promises Content ID for ambient sound. Keep your original recording files as proof of ownership, and use the copyright removal form for full re-uploads. If someone claims your own field recording through Content ID, dispute it.

findings.topic: Spam rule: automated mass production
findings.official_quote: Automated or synthetic mass-production: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don't allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content.
findings.applies: This is a Community Guidelines rule, so breaking it can bring warnings, strikes and termination, not just loss of monetization. The page's own example is "Channels that use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos". That is the common way ambient channels are built at volume. A few versions of one sound are allowed; churning out dozens of near-identical rain videos is not.
findings.action: Keep the upload pace to what you can record and mix by hand. Don't batch-generate videos that differ only in title or picture.

findings.topic: AI disclosure for generated music or realistic pictures
findings.official_quote: Creators must disclose GenAI content that: ... • Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. • Creates music that’s the main focus of the video. ... Note: Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money.
findings.applies: This only applies if AI is used. Examples are an AI-generated piano for "Slow Piano and Light Rain", or a photorealistic AI still of the library, tent or train. The same page warns that creators who "consistently choose not to disclose" may face "suspension from the YouTube Partner Program". Black-screen videos and the owner's own recordings need nothing.
findings.action: If the piano or a photorealistic picture is made with AI, set "AI use" to Yes when uploading. Otherwise set it to No.

review.audience_setting: Not made for kids. Rain and sleep sound is general-audience content, and YouTube says "General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”" A video is not made for kids just because "It’s safe or appropriate for everyone to watch" or because "Children may incidentally see it." Keep it that way by avoiding lullabies, nursery songs or cartoon characters in titles and pictures (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9528076).
review.notes:
I read every quote above on support.google.com through the reader; all pages loaded and none printed COULD NOT READ.

No official page mentions ambient, sleep, white-noise or still-image/black-screen videos by name. Blogs that say "static image videos are demonetized" or "rain channels can't be monetized" go further than YouTube's words. The official test is the "Generic or Repetitive Content" rule: each video's substance must be materially varied. The closest example, "Image slideshows, templated storylines, or scrolling text with minimal or no narrative, commentary, or educational value", is about slideshows, not a single still under original sound. So the sound has to carry each video's originality.

The monetization policies page now groups the old "repetitious/inauthentic" rule into sections called "Generic or Repetitive Content" and "Unsatisfying or Off-putting Content". The kit's phrase "the inauthentic-content rule" still matches YouTube's July 15, 2025 rename note on that page.

The spam page says "posting a few variations of a video is ok". So the 3-hour/8-hour pairs aren't a Community Guidelines problem, but they are a monetization risk under the generic/repetitive rule.

Distributors' pages (RouteNote, FUGA, Identity Music, Ditto) say nature and white-noise recordings are ineligible for Content ID. That is unofficial, but it agrees with YouTube's official "Sound effects, soundbeds, or production loops" line. TuneCore says otherwise.

Titles must deliver what they say ("8 Hours", "Black Screen"). The spam page's "Malicious clickbait" covers this, but it applies to every channel, so I didn't list it as a finding.

The Copyright Match Tool page (answer/7648743) describes finding re-uploads of your videos. I didn't confirm which channels can use it.

The kit's step 7 line against health claims is consistent with what I read; no change needed.

kept.topic: Generic or repetitive content (the renamed "inauthentic content" rule)
kept.official_quote: What’s important is that the substance of each video should be materially varied and deliver creative, educational, or other value. ... That means channels where content feels interchangeable from video to video are not allowed to monetize. ... Examples of what’s not allowed to monetize (this list is not exhaustive): • Similar or repetitive content with low educational value, commentary, narratives, or minimal variation across videos
kept.applies: Hours of rain with no voice and a still picture is about as exposed to this rule as a channel can be, because the sound is the only thing that makes one video different from the next. The ten titles are ten different sounds, which is good. But recipe step 5 says to publish every sound twice, once at 3 hours and once at 8. That would make half the catalogue near-copies of the other half, which risks being read as "minimal variation across videos". YouTube doesn't name two lengths of one sound as a violation; this is the cautious reading. The same page says reviewers "may focus on" a channel's "Main theme", "Most viewed videos", "Newest videos" and "Biggest proportion of watch time". On a channel of 8-hour videos, a few uploads will hold most of the watch time, so those should be the most clearly original. No official page names ambient, sleep or still-image videos as allowed or banned. The test is whether each video is materially varied.
kept.action: Give each sound one length, and make every upload a different recording or mix with its own place, layers and picture. Don't upload the same mix again at a second length.

kit_edit.quote: 5. Length. Publish one 3-hour and one 8-hour version of each sound.
kit_edit.replace_with: 5. Length. Give each sound one length, anywhere from 2 to 10 hours (YouTube's upload limit is 12 hours). Don't upload the same mix again at another length: two videos of the same sound can look interchangeable, and YouTube doesn't monetize channels where videos feel interchangeable.

kept.topic: Reused content: a licence or permission doesn't make it yours
kept.official_quote: Taking someone else’s content, making minimal changes, and calling it your own original work would be a violation of this guideline. If we cannot tell that the content is yours, it may be subject to our reused content policy. This policy applies even if you have permission from the original creator. Reused content is separate from YouTube’s Copyright enforcement, which means it’s not based on copyright, permission, or fair use. ... • Content uploaded many times by other creators ... • Content downloaded or copied from another online source without any substantive modifications
kept.applies: Recipe step 1 says sound "with a licence that allows commercial use on YouTube" is enough. A licence settles copyright, but not YouTube's reused-content rule, which the same page says is "not based on copyright, permission, or fair use." Stock and library rain, including YouTube's own Audio Library effects, can be used by many other channels. A video that is mostly one library rain track looped for hours risks counting as "Content downloaded or copied from another online source without any substantive modifications" or "Content uploaded many times by other creators", even with a licence. YouTube doesn't require you to record everything yourself, but your own recording is the safest way to show the work is yours.
kept.action: Make the main sound of every video your own recording where you can. Use a licensed sound only as one layer in your own mix, never as the whole video with little change, and keep every licence.

kit_edit.quote: 1. Sound. Use rain you record yourself, or sound with a licence that allows commercial use on YouTube. Keep the licence. Sound copied from another channel is what gets these channels demonetized.
kit_edit.replace_with: 1. Sound. Record the main sound of each video yourself where you can. A licensed sound can be one layer in your own mix, never the whole video with little change: a licence settles copyright, but YouTube's reused-content rule applies even with permission, and the same library rain can be on many other channels. Keep every licence. Never use sound copied from another channel.

kept.topic: Reused content is judged for the whole channel: show that you made it
kept.official_quote: To figure out whether your content is reused, our reviewers will check your channel to understand how you created, participated in, or produced your content. Our reviewers may check your channel’s: • Videos • Channel description • Video title • Video descriptions Our reused content policy applies to your channel as a whole. If you have videos that violate our guidelines, or if we cannot clearly tell that you made the content, monetization may be removed from your entire channel.
kept.applies: With no face and no voice, a reviewer can't see or hear who made the recording. The page lists the channel description, video titles and video descriptions among what reviewers may check, and it allows "Reused content from other online sources where the creator is either visible in the content or explains how the creator added to the content". So the description is where this channel shows it made the work. Recipe step 7 asks only for the sounds and the loop length, not how they were made.
kept.action: In every video description, say where and how the sound was recorded, what is layered in it and how long the loop is, and credit any licensed layer.

kit_edit.quote: 7. Description. Say what the sounds are and how long the loop is. Don't claim it treats insomnia, anxiety or any condition.
kit_edit.replace_with: 7. Description. Say what the sounds are, where and how you recorded them, what you layered together and how long the loop is, and credit any licensed sound. YouTube's reviewers may read descriptions to see how you made the content. Don't claim it treats insomnia, anxiety or any condition.

kept.topic: Music and sound licensing: only the Audio Library is known to be copyright-safe
kept.official_quote: If you’re using a track with a Creative Commons license, you must credit the artist in your video’s description. ... Copyright-safe music and sound effects downloaded from the Audio Library won't be claimed by a rights holder through the Content ID system. ... • Only music and sound effects from the Audio Library are known to YouTube to be copyright-safe. • YouTube is not responsible for issues that arise from “royalty-free” music and sound effects from YouTube channels or other music libraries.
kept.applies: The titles include "Slow Piano and Light Rain for Studying" and the About text lists "a slow piano". Any piano or sound layer the owner doesn't record or play himself comes from someone else, and YouTube takes no responsibility for claims on "royalty-free" sound from other libraries or channels. Audio Library sound won't be claimed through Content ID. The About text says "All sound here is recorded or made for this channel." That stops being true once a licensed layer is used.
kept.action: Play or compose the piano yourself, or use one licensed track as a layer. Prefer the YouTube Audio Library for any outside sound, and credit Creative Commons tracks in the description. Make the About text say only what is true.

kit_edit.quote: All sound here is recorded or made for this channel.
kit_edit.replace_with: All sound here is recorded or mixed for this channel. Each video's description says where it was recorded, what is layered in it, and credits any licensed sound.

kept.topic: Phone verification and the 12-hour limit for long uploads
kept.official_quote: By default, you can upload videos that are up to 15 minutes long. Verified accounts can upload videos longer than 15 minutes. ... The maximum file size you can upload is 256 GB or 12 hours, whichever is less. ... If you’ve verified your account, you’ll see "Enabled" in the Features that require a phone verification box. ... If you could previously upload long videos and no longer can, check your account for copyright claims and strikes .
kept.applies: Every planned video is 2 to 10 hours long, so nothing can be uploaded until the account is verified (by text message or automated voice call). Uploads over 12 hours aren't possible. The page links losing long uploads to copyright claims and strikes, so a strike from unlicensed sound would hit this channel harder than most.
kept.action: Verify the account at youtube.com/verify before the first upload, and check that Feature eligibility shows "Enabled" under features that require phone verification. Keep every video under 12 hours, and treat any copyright claim or strike as urgent.

kept.topic: Mid-roll ads on sleep videos
kept.official_quote: By default, automatic mid-roll ad slots are selected for your video. ... While YouTube can automatically suggest the best placement for mid-roll ads, you may want to turn off mid-roll ads if not appropriate. For example, meditation videos may not be suitable for mid-roll ads.
kept.applies: The channel promises "no sudden noises ... so nothing pulls you back". Once mid-rolls are switched on, YouTube places automatic slots by default, and ads during an 8-hour sleep video would break that promise. YouTube itself names meditation videos as a case where mid-rolls may not suit.
kept.action: Once monetized, decide on purpose. Either leave mid-roll ads off for sleep videos, or place a few manual slots and untick "Automatic ad slots". Don't accept the automatic slots without deciding.

kept.topic: Content ID likely can't protect rain and noise beds
kept.official_quote: The features described in this article are available only to partners who use YouTube's Content ID matching system. ... You must have exclusive rights to the material in the reference file for the territories where you claim ownership. The following examples are ineligible for use in or as a reference: • Content licensed non-exclusively from a third party • Content released under Creative Commons or similar free of charge/open licenses ... All reference content must be sufficiently distinct. • Karaoke recordings, remasters, sound-alike recordings, and some dubbed content • Sound effects, soundbeds, or production loops
kept.applies: YouTube lists "Sound effects, soundbeds, or production loops" as not distinct enough for Content ID, so rain, wind and noise beds most likely can't be registered, even through a distributor. Licensed or Creative Commons layers can never be registered. Re-uploads by other channels won't be caught by Content ID. The same rule means nobody else should be claiming a generic soundbed either. Distributor pages saying nature and white-noise recordings are ineligible are unofficial but agree with this line.
kept.action: Don't pay a distributor that promises Content ID for ambient sound. Keep your original recording files as proof that you made them, and report full re-uploads with the copyright removal request form. If someone claims your own field recording through Content ID and you hold all the rights, dispute the claim.

kept.topic: Spam rule: automated mass production
kept.official_quote: Automated or synthetic mass-production: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don't allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content. This includes coordinated mass-production and technical manipulation to bypass filters or trick viewers. • Example: Channels that use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos, with each video reading out an AI-generated script.
kept.applies: This is a Community Guidelines rule, so breaking it can lead to suspended monetization, warnings, strikes or termination, not just lost ads. YouTube's own example also involves AI-written scripts read aloud, which this channel doesn't have. The part that matters here is "high volumes of similar content with minimal changes": a few versions of one sound are fine, but dozens of near-identical rain videos are not.
kept.action: Upload only as fast as you can record and mix by hand. Don't batch-generate videos that differ only in title or picture.

kept.topic: AI disclosure for generated music, sound or realistic pictures
kept.official_quote: Creators must disclose GenAI content that: ... • Generates a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur. • Creates music that’s the main focus of the video. ... AI content can include content that is fully or partially altered or created using any AI audio, video, image creation or editing tools. Realistic AI content and meaningful changes require disclosure, while non-realistic or minor edits don’t. ... Note: Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money. ... Creators who consistently choose not to disclose this information may be subject to manual application of a label, or penalties from YouTube, including removal of content or suspension from the YouTube Partner Program.
kept.applies: This only matters if AI is used: for example an AI-generated piano for "Slow Piano and Light Rain", AI-generated rain or train sound meant to sound real, or a photorealistic AI picture of the library, tent or train. The page says noise clean-up on your own recordings needs no disclosure ("Using effects to enhance previously recorded audio"). Black-screen videos and the owner's own unedited recordings need nothing.
kept.action: If the music, a realistic sound bed or a photorealistic picture is made with AI, set "AI use" to Yes when uploading. Otherwise set it to No.

added.topic: Rights to the still image and to samples and loops
added.official_quote: Also ensure that you have all the necessary rights to commercially use all visual and audio elements in your content. ... If you used samples or loops, make sure that the license specifically allows for their commercial use. ... Sometimes rights owners require you to credit the creator of the content or give proof of purchase to use it in your video for commercial purposes. ... Although you may have found the content online free of charge, usually its actual creator holds many of the rights needed to commercially exploit the content.
added.applies: The review covers sound licensing but not the picture. Recipe step 4 says "One still image" without saying where it comes from. A rain, library or tent photo found online is not free to monetize just because it was free to download, and sample packs need a licence that allows commercial use.
added.action: Use your own photos, or images licensed for commercial use, and keep the licence or proof of purchase. Check that any sample or loop pack allows commercial use.

kit_edit.quote: 4. Picture. One still image or a black screen. Say "black screen" in the title when it is one: people search for it.
kit_edit.replace_with: 4. Picture. One still image or a black screen. Use a photo you took or one licensed for commercial use, and keep the licence: a picture found online isn't yours to monetize. Say "black screen" in the title when it is one: people search for it.

added.topic: No slowed-down songs or playlists of other people's tracks
added.official_quote: More examples of what’s not allowed to monetize (this list is not exhaustive): ... • Collections of songs from different artists (even if you have their permission) ... • Songs modified to change the pitch or speed, but are otherwise identical to the original song
added.applies: The niche includes lofi and a slow piano. A common shortcut is to slow down an existing track or string library songs together under rain. YouTube lists both as reused content that can't be monetized, even with permission. (The original review cited the song-collections line as being on the Audio Library page; it is on this monetization policies page.)
added.action: Make the piano or lofi part yourself, or use one licensed track as a layer. Never slow down or re-pitch an existing song, and never make a playlist of other artists' tracks.

added.topic: Finding full re-uploads: the Copyright Match Tool
added.official_quote: The Copyright Match Tool scans for full reuploads of your videos on other YouTube channels. The tool scans videos uploaded after yours, so it’s important you’re the first one to upload the content to YouTube. ... The Copyright Match Tool is available to any channel that’s filled out a valid copyright removal request ... For channels in the YouTube Partner Program (YPP), the tool is available on the Copyright page in YouTube Studio ... Misuse of the Copyright Match Tool may result in loss of feature access or termination of your YouTube account or partnership.
added.applies: Content ID likely won't protect rain beds, so this tool is the official way to catch whole-video copies of this channel's uploads. It only finds copies uploaded after yours, and it opens to a channel once it joins the Partner Program or files a valid copyright removal request.
added.action: Upload each recording to this channel before sharing it anywhere else. Report full copies with the copyright removal request form and check the Matches tab after. Only report real copies of your own recordings: misuse can cost the tool or the channel.

proved.audience_setting: Not made for kids. Rain and sleep sound is general-audience content, and YouTube says \"General audience content should be set as “not made for kids.”\" YouTube also says \"a video is not necessarily made for kids just because\" \"It’s safe or appropriate for everyone to watch\" or \"Children may incidentally see it.\" Keep it that way: no lullabies, nursery songs, cartoon characters or child-directed wording in titles and pictures, because \"songs, stories, or poems for children\" and \"characters ... that appeal to children\" are factors that make a video made for kids. Setting it correctly is the creator's legal responsibility under COPPA (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9528076).
proved.notes:
I re-read every quote on the official pages through the reader. All pages loaded and none printed COULD NOT READ. Every finding was confirmed, so nothing was struck. These corrections were made:
- Generic/repetitive: the kit_edit's lengths now cover the 2- and 10-hour titles. "Exactly what YouTube names" is softened to "risks", because YouTube doesn't name two lengths of one sound. The reviewers "may" focus on these items; they don't always.
- Reused content: added the closer example, "Content downloaded or copied from another online source without any substantive modifications". "Is used by many other channels" is now "can be". The action no longer says YouTube requires self-recording: own recording is the safest route, and licensed sound is fine as a layer with substantive changes.
- Show you made it: the page says reviewers "may check" descriptions; the replace_with now says "may" too.
- Audio Library: the "Collections of songs from different artists" line is on answer/1311392, not answer/3376882, so I moved it into a new added finding. I also added the line that Audio Library sound won't be claimed through Content ID.
- Mid-rolls: "keep pre-roll only" is removed. The page says nothing about choosing pre-roll, and automatic slots are the default only once mid-rolls are switched on.
- Content ID: the original quote ran two sections together. "Sound effects, soundbeds, or production loops" sits under "All reference content must be sufficiently distinct", not under exclusive rights. The topic is softened from "can't" to "likely can't". The page also applies only to Content ID partners.
- Spam: the quoted example was cut short. The full example also involves "each video reading out an AI-generated script", so I dropped the claim that it describes how ambient channels are usually built.
- AI disclosure: added realistic AI-generated sound beds, and the page's own exemption for enhancing audio you recorded.
- Audience: the page says a video is "not necessarily" made for kids just because it is family-friendly; the review had left out "necessarily".
- Added: rights to the still image and to samples (answer/2490020, with a kit_edit to step 4); slowed or re-pitched songs and song collections (answer/1311392); and the Copyright Match Tool for re-uploads (answer/15269184).
- Static image: a search of YouTube Help found no official page that names static-image, ambient or sleep videos. The review's statement that blogs saying \"static image videos are demonetized\" go beyond YouTube's words stands.
- I didn't add the Partner Program eligibility thresholds. They aren't specific to this format, and I didn't re-read that page.

review.audience_setting: Made for kids, set at the channel level. YouTube says "If your video features actors, characters, activities, games, songs, stories, or other subject matter that reflect an intent to target children, it’s likely made for kids." These wordless picture-book stories, with cute animated snails, pebbles, candles and clouds and a soft marimba, match YouTube's listed factors ("animated characters or cartoon figures", "songs, stories, or poems for children"). Even if adults also watch, YouTube counts mixed-audience content as "a type of made for kids content".

findings.topic: Made for kids (COPPA) audience setting
findings.official_quote: If your video features actors, characters, activities, games, songs, stories, or other subject matter that reflect an intent to target children, it’s likely made for kids. / Whether the video includes characters, celebrities, or toys that appeal to children, including animated characters or cartoon figures. / Mixed audience content, on the other hand, is considered a type of made for kids content.
findings.applies: The channel's characters are cute animated objects and small animals, and the titles read like children's picture books ("The Candle Who Was Afraid of the Dark", "The Little Cloud That Couldn't Rain"). The stories teach simple lessons, like sharing the leaf. That hits several of YouTube's factors. YouTube does list "Animated content that appeals to everyone" as general audience, and "family friendly" alone doesn't make a video made for kids. But that only holds "in the absence of information suggesting an intent to target kids", and here the whole style points at kids. YouTube also says it "may override your audience setting choice in cases of error or abuse", so choosing "not made for kids" would likely be overruled and could bring legal trouble under COPPA.
findings.action: On a computer, open YouTube Studio and go to Settings > Channel > Advanced settings > Audience. Choose "Yes, set this channel as made for kids. I mostly upload content that's made for kids." YouTube says it cannot give legal advice and suggests a lawyer if he is unsure.

findings.topic: What made for kids switches off (ads, comments, bell, memberships)
findings.official_quote: Most importantly, we don’t serve personalized ads on kids content, as required by the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and/or other applicable laws. Not serving personalized ads on kids content may result in a decrease in revenue for some creators who mark their content as made for kids.
findings.applies: The same page lists features that turn off on made-for-kids videos, including "Comments", "Notification bell", "Personalized advertising", "Save to playlist and Save to watch later", "Channel Memberships" and "Cards or end screens". A channel set as made for kids also loses "Posts". Ads can still run, but only contextual ones: "Contextual ads can be served on YouTube for supervised accounts and on content set as made for kids" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/9713557). So every view earns less, nobody can comment, and the channel can't build a community or get viewer feedback in comments. The script's "END CARD" is fine only as the last frame of the animation itself, not as a YouTube end screen.
findings.action: Plan growth around the Shorts feed and recommendations alone. Don't plan on comments, the bell, playlists, memberships or community Posts, and don't ask viewers to comment or tap the bell. Animate the script's END CARD into the video.

findings.topic: Shorts revenue thresholds from Feb 1, 2027 (Shorts-only, made for kids)
findings.official_quote: To earn each month from the Shorts Creator Pool, creators will now need to maintain 10M qualified Shorts views over the last 90 days. If you miss this threshold, you will not be removed from YPP and this will not impact other YPP earnings, including long-form video. / Starting Feb. 1, 2027, YPP entry thresholds for new creators are changing to 8,000 qualified watch hours in the last 365 days, or 20M qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days, in addition to still needing 1k subscribers.
findings.applies: This channel is more exposed than most, for two reasons. First, it posts only Shorts, so a month under 10M Shorts views in 90 days earns no Shorts ad money at all. Second, it is made for kids, which closes the smaller earning routes: channel memberships require "Channel isn’t set as Made for Kids" and Shopping requires "Channel isn’t set as Made for Kids and doesn’t have a significant number of videos set as made for kids" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/72857). Ads (contextual only) are left as the main income. A new channel joining after Feb 1, 2027 needs 20M Shorts views in 90 days, or 8,000 watch hours. Watch hours from the Shorts feed don't count toward that (support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851). The YouTube Blog (Aug 10, 2026) confirms channels below the Shorts threshold "continue earning on long-form content".
findings.action: Don't build the money plan on Shorts revenue alone. Add longer original episodes (or long videos collecting his own episodes) so the channel can reach the 8,000 watch-hour route and earn watch-page ads. If the channel is in YPP before then, accept the updated terms in YouTube Studio by January 31, 2027.

findings.topic: Inauthentic content: same storyline, same outcome
findings.official_quote: Videos where characters are put in the same situation over and over again with the same outcome (i.e., using a highly similar storyline template across multiple videos) / Similar content, like a series following a set of characters across episodes or a channel that does product reviews, but in which each video has a distinct storyline, focus, or concept / AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective
findings.applies: The first quote is on YouTube's list of what can't earn money. The second is on its list of what can. The kit's premise is one formula, "tiny characters doing difficult things": a tiny hero meets a huge obstacle, fails, tries again and makes it. The snail script follows that arc, and most of the ten titles invite it (pebble/hill, raindrop/home, ant/crumb, seed/pavement). Ten episodes with the same arc and the same win would match the first quote. YouTube's reviewers look at the "Main theme" and the "Channel’s “About” section", and the current description announces the formula. If AI tools make the animation, the same page allows "using AI to visualize a unique character and narrative you invented", but not templated mass production.
findings.action: Before production, write one line per episode giving its concept and its ending, and make sure no two share the same arc. Vary the endings: some heroes don't make it but find something better, some help another character, some change their minds. Use the description below so it promises varied stories.

kit_edit.quote: Animated shorts about tiny characters doing difficult things: a snail crossing a road, a pebble climbing a hill, a raindrop trying to get home.
kit_edit.replace_with: Animated stories about tiny characters and their big days: a snail who finds a friend at the end of a long road, a candle who is scared of the dark, a paper boat that meets the sea. Every episode is a new story with its own ending.

findings.topic: Inauthentic content: animals in distress or peril
findings.official_quote: Channels that heavily rely on generic templates or emotionally manipulative themes, like a series showing repetitive scenarios of animals in exaggerated distress or peril
findings.applies: This is on YouTube's list of what can't earn money. The heroes are small animals and fragile things (a snail on a road, an ant, a raindrop). The snail script's bicycle-wheel moment is brief and comic, which is fine. The risk is the series sliding into danger as its recurring hook, such as a creature about to be crushed in the opening shot or the thumbnail.
findings.action: Keep danger brief and gentle, and never the main hook. No episode or thumbnail should be built around a creature about to be crushed, drowned or lost. Open on the hero's goal or curiosity instead.

findings.topic: Child safety: death and violence in family cartoons
findings.official_quote: Family friendly cartoons that target young minors and contain adult or age-inappropriate themes such as violence, sex, death, drugs, and more. We don’t allow content labeled as suitable for kids in the video's title, description, tags, or in the audience selection if it contains age-inappropriate themes.
findings.applies: This is a Community Guidelines rule, so breaking it means the video is removed, not just fewer ads. The characters' natural endings are often deaths: a last leaf falling, a candle burning out, a raindrop drying up, a paper boat sinking, a snail under a wheel. With the audience set to made for kids, showing any of those on screen could get a video removed and the channel a strike. Age-appropriate treatment of loss is allowed (YouTube Kids' Preschool setting accepts "loss and grief" handled gently), but on-screen death or injury isn't.
findings.action: No character dies, gets crushed, melts away, burns out or sinks on screen. Give "The Last Leaf Refuses to Fall", "The Candle Who Was Afraid of the Dark" and "A Paper Boat Meets the Sea" gentle endings where the hero changes or finds a new place, not one where it ends.

findings.topic: Quality principles for kids and family content
findings.official_quote: If a channel is found to have a strong focus on low-quality “made for kids” content, it may be suspended from the YouTube Partner Program. / Hard to follow: Videos that are confusing or make no sense, often due to jumbled storylines, unclear audio, or lack of clear storyline (beginning, middle & end). This type of video is often the result of mass production or autogeneration.
findings.applies: Once the channel is made for kids, these principles decide its ad status. YouTube currently enforces six of them (support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392), and the page says they apply to Shorts. With no words, the pictures alone must carry a clear beginning, middle and end, and AI-stitched clips are the usual way videos become "hard to follow". The snail script passes: it has a clear arc and ends with the snails sharing the leaf, which matches YouTube's high-quality example of "demonstrating kindness, good friendship". One more enforced principle is "Encouraging negative behaviors or attitudes: Content that encourages dangerous activities". YouTube's examples are pranks and unhealthy eating, so a cartoon snail on a road isn't a clear case. Still, a hero setting off across a road with bikes passing could read as unsafe to young viewers.
findings.action: Before uploading, watch each episode without knowing its title. If the beginning, middle and end aren't obvious from the pictures alone, fix it. Optional, at no cost: in the snail script, have it look left, then right before it sets off across the road (2-6s), so it shows a safe habit.

findings.topic: YouTube Kids app
findings.official_quote: Videos set as “made for kids” are not automatically included in the YouTube Kids app.
findings.applies: There is no application; YouTube picks videos "using a mix of automated filters, user feedback, and human review". Gentle wordless shorts suit the Preschool and Younger settings. The Preschool rules (support.google.com/youtube/answer/10938174) ask for "Non-violent and non-scary scripted and animated videos" and say videos there "don’t feature graphic imagery or extreme sadness, anger, or fear". So the bicycle moment, the candle's fear of the dark and the cloud that can't rain need to stay mild. YouTube Kids also excludes branded content, product-focused videos, and misleading, sensational or keyword-stuffed titles and thumbnails. The current titles are plain and fine.
findings.action: Do nothing to apply. Keep fear and sadness mild and resolved within the episode, never put brands or products in episodes, and keep titles and thumbnails as plain as the current ten.

findings.topic: AI disclosure (AI-made animation and music)
findings.official_quote: Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI, or edits to realistic content that are minor. / Using an AI-generated or altered animation of a missile in a fully animated video / Creates music that’s the main focus of the video.
findings.applies: A stylised 3D snail paddling with a flag is clearly not realistic, so AI-made animation needs no disclosure. Two things change that. The page's must-disclose examples include "AI generated music" with no further qualifier, which would cover an AI-made marimba line. A photorealistic real road or real rain could count as "a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur". YouTube adds that "Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money". It may also label videos automatically if its systems detect AI or the file carries C2PA data.
findings.action: At upload, under Attributes > AI use, choose No when the visuals are stylised and the music is made by a person or licensed. Choose Yes if the music is AI-generated or the visuals look photorealistic. Keep the stylised look.

review.notes:
I didn't find any official page saying whether made-for-kids Shorts share in the Shorts feed revenue pool. The Shorts monetization page (12504220) doesn't mention made for kids. The official pages say only that made-for-kids content gets contextual ads, not personalised ones.

Super Thanks has no made-for-kids rule on the official requirements page. It shows in the comments section, though, and comments are off on made-for-kids videos, so it probably won't work here. That is my inference, not an official statement.

The Feb 1, 2027 YPP changes are announced but not yet in force (help page 12843009 and the YouTube Blog post of Aug 10, 2026). The general YPP page (72851) still lists today's 4,000 watch hours or 10M Shorts views.

One URL I guessed, support.google.com/youtube/answer/11089305, printed COULD NOT READ (HTTP 404); I used nothing from it. All quotes above come from pages the reader printed.

Kit inconsistency, not a rule problem: the script's notes say to keep the snail and its flag in every episode, but titles 2-10 star other heroes (a pebble, a raindrop, an ant, a candle...). YouTube allows either a recurring cast or an anthology as long as each video has a distinct story, so the owner should choose one. One option is the snail appearing in each episode beside that episode's hero.

The closing line \"All characters and stories are original to this channel.\" is worth keeping: reviewers read the About section when they check for reused content. None of the ten titles has keyword stuffing or misleading claims.

proved.audience_setting: Made for kids, set for the whole channel. This is a judgment call that YouTube leaves to the creator: it "cannot provide legal advice" and says that including some of its factors "does not automatically mean it’s made for kids". Still, this kit matches several of YouTube's factors: "characters ... that appeal to children, including animated characters or cartoon figures" and "songs, stories, or poems for children". It has picture-book titles, cute snails, pebbles, candles and clouds, small lessons like sharing the leaf, and a soft marimba. Content that "targets children as one of its audiences, even if it’s not the main or primary audience" counts as mixed audience, which YouTube treats as "a type of made for kids content". "Animated content that appeals to everyone" counts as general audience only "in the absence of information suggesting an intent to target kids". Choosing made for kids is the safer reading of this kit. YouTube "may override your audience setting choice in cases of error or abuse", and setting it wrongly "might" bring legal consequences under COPPA.

kept.topic: Made for kids (COPPA) audience setting
kept.official_quote: If your video features actors, characters, activities, games, songs, stories, or other subject matter that reflect an intent to target children, it’s likely made for kids. / Whether the video includes characters, celebrities, or toys that appeal to children, including animated characters or cartoon figures. / Mixed audience content, on the other hand, is considered a type of made for kids content. / Just because your content may include some of these factors does not automatically mean it’s made for kids.
kept.applies: Corrected: the review said a "not made for kids" choice "would likely be overruled", which goes further than YouTube does. YouTube's words are "we may override your audience setting choice in cases of error or abuse" and "If you don’t set your audience as made for kids accurately, you might face legal consequences or consequences on YouTube" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/9527654). The kit's characters are cute animated objects and small animals, and the titles read like picture books ("The Candle Who Was Afraid of the Dark", "The Little Cloud That Couldn't Rain"). The stories teach small lessons. That matches several of YouTube's factors. "Family friendly" on its own doesn't make a video made for kids, and "Animated content that appeals to everyone" can be general audience, but only "in the absence of information suggesting an intent to target kids". This kit has that kind of information.
kept.action: On a computer, sign in to studio.youtube.com and go to Settings > Channel > Advanced settings > Audience. Choose "Yes, set this channel as made for kids. I mostly upload content that’s made for kids." YouTube says it cannot give legal advice and suggests a lawyer if he is unsure. If he wants a general-audience channel instead, the titles, look and stories would have to stop targeting children, and this kit would need rewriting.

kept.topic: What made for kids switches off (ads, comments, bell, memberships)
kept.official_quote: Most importantly, we don’t serve personalized ads on kids content, as required by the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and/or other applicable laws. Not serving personalized ads on kids content may result in a decrease in revenue for some creators who mark their content as made for kids.
kept.applies: Corrected: the review said "every view earns less". YouTube says it "may result in a decrease in revenue for some creators". The same page lists features that aren't available on made-for-kids videos, including "Cards or end screens", "Channel Memberships", "Comments", "Notification bell", "Personalized advertising", "Playback in the Miniplayer" and "Save to playlist and Save to watch later". A channel set as made for kids also loses "Posts" and "Ask Studio". Ads still run, but only contextual ones: "Contextual ads can be served on YouTube for supervised accounts and on content set as made for kids" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/9713557). On the plus side, "Videos that you set as “made for kids” are more likely to be recommended alongside other kids’ videos" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/9528076). The script's END CARD works only as the last frame of the animation, not as a YouTube end screen.
kept.action: Plan growth around the Shorts feed and recommendations next to other kids' videos. Don't count on comments, the bell, viewers saving to playlists, memberships or community Posts, and don't ask viewers to comment or tap the bell. Animate the END CARD into the video itself.

kept.topic: Shorts revenue thresholds from Feb 1, 2027 (Shorts-only, made for kids)
kept.official_quote: To earn each month from the Shorts Creator Pool, creators will now need to maintain 10M qualified Shorts views over the last 90 days. If you miss this threshold, you will not be removed from YPP and this will not impact other YPP earnings, including long-form video. / Starting Feb. 1, 2027, YPP entry thresholds for new creators are changing to 8,000 qualified watch hours in the last 365 days, or 20M qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days, in addition to still needing 1k subscribers.
kept.applies: Confirmed. The Shorts monetization page adds that from Feb 1, 2027 a channel needs at least 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days "to be eligible to earn a share of Shorts ad revenue from the Creator Pool and YouTube Premium revenue for each month" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/12504220). The YouTube Blog (Aug 10, 2026) says channels below it "remain in YPP and continue earning on long-form content". This channel posts only Shorts, so a 90-day stretch under 10M views means no Shorts ad or Premium money that month. Made for kids also closes other ways to earn. Channel memberships require "Channel isn’t set as Made for Kids and doesn’t have a significant number of ineligible videos". Shopping requires "Channel isn’t set as Made for Kids and doesn’t have a significant number of videos set as made for kids" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/72857). A new channel joining after Feb 1, 2027 needs 1,000 subscribers plus 20M Shorts views in 90 days or 8,000 watch hours in 365 days. YouTube says Shorts-feed watch hours "won’t count towards the 4,000 qualified public watch hours threshold" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851). That page hasn't been updated for the 8,000 figure. Both thresholds use the same term, "qualified watch hours", so the same exclusion very likely applies, but that is an inference.
kept.action: Don't base the money plan on Shorts revenue alone. Add longer original episodes so the channel can reach the watch-hour route and earn watch-page ads. If the channel somehow joins YPP before Feb 1, 2027, accept the updated terms in YouTube Studio by January 31, 2027.

kept.topic: Generic or repetitive content (YouTube's "inauthentic content"): same storyline, same outcome
kept.official_quote: Videos where characters are put in the same situation over and over again with the same outcome (i.e., using a highly similar storyline template across multiple videos) / Similar content, like a series following a set of characters across episodes or a channel that does product reviews, but in which each video has a distinct storyline, focus, or concept / AI-generated content made with generic or unoriginal templates giving the impression of mass production without adding the creator’s original, authentic insights or perspective
kept.applies: Confirmed. YouTube renamed this policy "inauthentic content" on July 15, 2025, and the page now heads the section "Generic or Repetitive Content". The first and third quotes are on the list of what can't earn money; the second is on the list of what can. The kit's premise, "tiny characters doing difficult things", plus the script note to "keep this snail and its flag in every episode" and the snail's arc (meets an obstacle, fails, tries again, makes it), could add up to the same situation with the same outcome. Corrected wording: YouTube's reviewers "may focus on" the channel's "Main theme", its metadata and its "Channel’s “About” section". A recurring cast is allowed, and the current description breaks no rule by itself. Rewording it is a sensible precaution, not a requirement. AI animation is fine when it is "using AI to visualize a unique character and narrative you invented".
kept.action: Before production, write one line per episode giving its concept and its ending, and make sure no two share the same arc. Vary the endings: some heroes find something better than their goal, some help someone else, some change their minds. Use the description below so it promises varied stories.

kit_edit.quote: Animated shorts about tiny characters doing difficult things: a snail crossing a road, a pebble climbing a hill, a raindrop trying to get home.
kit_edit.replace_with: Animated stories about tiny characters and their big days: a snail who finds a friend at the end of a long road, a candle who is scared of the dark, a paper boat that meets the sea. Every episode is a new story with its own ending.

kept.topic: Unsatisfying content: peril and loss as the hook
kept.official_quote: Channels that heavily rely on generic templates or emotionally manipulative themes, like a series showing repetitive scenarios of animals in exaggerated distress or peril / Content that repeatedly uses disturbing themes (such as violence or loss) without building a cohesive narrative
kept.applies: Corrected label: both quotes are under YouTube's "Unsatisfying or Off-putting Content" heading, not under inauthentic content. Both are examples of content that can't earn money ("Channels that do not meet that bar will not be eligible for the YouTube Partner Program"). The heroes are small animals and fragile things. The snail script's bicycle-wheel moment is brief and comic, so it's fine. The risk is the series turning danger or loss into its recurring hook: a creature about to be crushed in the opening shot or thumbnail, or a run of sad endings with no real story.
kept.action: Keep danger brief and gentle and never the main hook. No episode or thumbnail should be built around a creature about to be crushed, drowned or lost. Open on the hero's goal or curiosity, and when an episode touches loss, give it a complete story with a hopeful turn.

kept.topic: Child safety: death and violence in family cartoons
kept.official_quote: Family friendly cartoons that target young minors and contain adult or age-inappropriate themes such as violence, sex, death, drugs, and more. We don’t allow content labeled as suitable for kids in the video's title, description, tags, or in the audience selection if it contains age-inappropriate themes. / Content that targets young minors and families with age-inappropriate themes within an educational, documentary, scientific, or artistic context may receive an exception. This is not a pass to target young minors and families with mature themes intended to shock young audiences.
kept.applies: Confirmed. This is a Community Guidelines rule, so a breach means removal, not just fewer ads ("we will remove the content"). Corrected: the review said a breach could bring the channel a strike. YouTube says "If this is your first time violating our Community Guidelines, you'll likely get a warning with no penalty to your channel"; strikes follow repeat violations. The rule covers age-inappropriate death and violence, not every mention of loss. YouTube Kids' Preschool setting accepts "Age-appropriate videos that discuss sensitive issues such as natural disasters, bullying, loss and grief" without "graphic imagery or extreme sadness, anger, or fear" (support.google.com/youtube/answer/10938174). The current script has no death. But several titles invite an ending that is a death (the last leaf, the candle, the paper boat, the raindrop), and with the audience set to made for kids, showing that on screen is the risk.
kept.action: No character dies, gets crushed, melts away, burns out or sinks on screen. Give "The Last Leaf Refuses to Fall", "The Candle Who Was Afraid of the Dark" and "A Paper Boat Meets the Sea" gentle endings where the hero changes or finds a new place.

kept.topic: Quality principles for kids and family content
kept.official_quote: If a channel is found to have a strong focus on low-quality “made for kids” content, it may be suspended from the YouTube Partner Program. / Hard to follow: Videos that are confusing or make no sense, often due to jumbled storylines, unclear audio, or lack of clear storyline (beginning, middle & end). This type of video is often the result of mass production or autogeneration. / High-quality “made for kids” content gets raised up in recommendations.
kept.applies: Confirmed. The principles "apply to both long-form content and YouTube Shorts". YouTube currently enforces six of them for monetization, all listed on support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392. Corrected: the review called AI-stitched clips "the usual way" videos become hard to follow. YouTube says only "often the result of mass production or autogeneration". It separately names "videos that stitch together unrelated or inconsistent AI clips" as content that can't earn money (1311392). With no words, the pictures alone must show a clear beginning, middle and end. The snail script does: it ends with sharing the leaf, which fits YouTube's high-quality example of "demonstrating kindness, good friendship". Another enforced principle covers content that "encourages dangerous activities". YouTube's examples are pranks and unhealthy eating, so a cartoon snail crossing a road isn't a clear case. The script already has the snail look left, then right, at the puddle (16-21s).
kept.action: Before uploading, watch each episode without knowing its title. If the beginning, middle and end aren't obvious from the pictures alone, fix it. Optional, at no cost: have the snail also look left, then right before it first sets off across the road (2-6s).

kept.topic: YouTube Kids app
kept.official_quote: Videos set as “made for kids” are not automatically included in the YouTube Kids app.
kept.applies: Corrected: YouTube describes no way to apply. It says "We use a mix of automated filters, user feedback, and human review to decide whether content is suitable for the YouTube Kids app." The Preschool setting (support.google.com/youtube/answer/10938174) asks for "Non-violent and non-scary scripted and animated videos" and says videos there "don’t feature graphic imagery or extreme sadness, anger, or fear". YouTube Kids also turns away branded content, overly commercial content, and "Misleading titles and thumbnails", "Sensational titles and thumbnails" and "Keyword stuffing in titles". The current ten titles are plain and fine.
kept.action: Nothing to apply for. Keep fear and sadness mild and resolved within each episode, keep brands and products out, and keep titles and thumbnails as plain as the current ten.

kept.topic: AI disclosure (AI-made animation and music)
kept.official_quote: Creators don’t need to disclose non-realistic content that’s made with AI, or edits to realistic content that are minor. / Using an AI-generated or altered animation of a missile in a fully animated video / Creates music that’s the main focus of the video. / AI generated music / Disclosing AI content alone won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money.
kept.applies: A stylised 3D snail is clearly not realistic, so AI-made animation needs no disclosure. Corrected on music: the review said "AI generated music" carries "no further qualifier" and covers any AI marimba line. YouTube's actual rule is to disclose AI that "Creates music that’s the main focus of the video", while its examples list just says "AI generated music". Whether a background marimba in a wordless cartoon is "the main focus" is unclear. Since disclosure "won’t limit a video’s audience or impact its eligibility to earn money", saying Yes is the safe choice. Not disclosing has a cost: "Creators who consistently choose not to disclose this information may be subject to manual application of a label, or penalties from YouTube, including removal of content or suspension from the YouTube Partner Program." Photorealistic real roads or real rain could count as "a realistic scene that didn’t actually occur". YouTube may also label a video automatically, for example when the file carries C2PA metadata, and that label can't be changed.
kept.action: At upload, under Attributes > AI use, choose No when the visuals are stylised and the music is made by a person or licensed. Choose Yes when the music is AI-generated or the visuals look photorealistic. Keep the stylised look.

added.topic: Super Thanks and Hype don't work on made-for-kids content
added.official_quote: Channel isn’t set as Made for Kids and doesn’t have a significant number of videos set as made for kids or ineligible / Super Thanks is not available for the following types of long-form videos and Shorts: / Made for kids
added.applies: The review's notes said no official page ties Super Thanks to made for kids. One does: the Super Thanks page shuts it off for channels set as made for kids and for each made-for-kids Short. The hype page (support.google.com/youtube/answer/15509925) lists "Made for kids content" among "Content that is not eligible for hype", so fans can't hype these Shorts either. With the channel set as made for kids, Super Thanks and hype are both out, along with memberships and Shopping.
added.action: Leave Super Thanks and hype out of the income and growth plans for this channel, and don't ask viewers to use them.

findings.topic: Phone verification: 2 channels per number per year
findings.official_quote: We use the phone number to send you a verification code. We also make sure the phone number is linked to no more than 2 channels per year. [...] To help prevent abuse, a phone number can only be associated with 2 channels per year.
findings.applies: All ten channels need phone verification. Without it a channel can't post videos longer than 15 minutes or use custom thumbnails. It is also the first step towards monetizing. The same page says: "To access advanced features, you must first complete phone verification. Then, you can choose to build up sufficient channel history or verification using ID or video." The YPP page lists "Have advanced features access on YouTube." as a requirement (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851). With one phone number, only two of the ten channels can be verified in a year, so ten would take five years. YouTube's own fix is on https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9891124: "If you've already verified 2 channels with 1 phone number, you must verify a different phone number." No official page says the limit counts per Google Account rather than per channel, so plan for it per channel. With Brand Accounts, only the primary owner can do ID or video verification (same page: "Only primary channel owners can verify their identity to get access to additional features.").
findings.action: Verify the first two channels with your main phone number now. Verify more channels in the same year only with another number you really own and will keep, since it doubles as a recovery number. Never use a borrowed or temporary number. Otherwise wait a year. Check Studio, Settings, Channel, Feature eligibility on each channel before planning uploads that need long videos or custom thumbnails.

kit_edit.quote: • Verify the channel with your phone number (Settings, Channel, Feature eligibility) so you can upload long videos and custom thumbnails.
kit_edit.replace_with: • Verify the channel with your phone number (Settings, Channel, Feature eligibility) so you can upload long videos and custom thumbnails. YouTube lets one phone number verify only 2 channels a year, so verify your first two channels now. Each further channel needs a different phone number you own, or has to wait a year. Every channel needs this step before it can ever be monetized.

findings.topic: A strike or termination on one channel reaches all ten
findings.official_quote: If your YouTube channel is terminated, you are prohibited from using, possessing, or creating any other YouTube channels. You are also prohibited from letting others whose YouTube channels have been terminated use your YouTube channel to bypass their termination. This applies to all of your existing channels, any new channels you create or acquire, and any channels in which you are repeatedly or prominently featured.
findings.applies: One person owns all ten channels, so if one is terminated he loses the right to use the other nine. Termination doesn't always need three strikes: "Sometimes a single case of severe abuse will result in channel termination without warning." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2802032; the spam policy names spam as one of these). Smaller problems also spread. "Videos with Community Guidelines strikes, copyright strikes, and videos with visuals matching third-party content may contribute to monetization suspension on all your related accounts." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/1727191). "Violation of our YouTube channel monetization policies may result in monetization being suspended or permanently disabled on all or any of your accounts." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392). The same page adds: "If any of your channels have been demonetized or terminated, you should not create new (or use existing) channels to get around these restrictions, or apply to YPP with related channels during your suspension period. Doing so could lead to termination of all channels." The kit's wording ("can put the others on the account at risk") is right but understates this.
findings.action: Treat all ten channels as one account at risk. Use only music, footage and sound you made or hold a commercial licence for, and keep the licences. If any channel gets a strike or loses monetization, pause new uploads everywhere, fix or appeal it, and don't apply any other channel to YPP while the suspension lasts. Never open a replacement channel.

kit_edit.quote: Uploading templated videos to ten at once is what YouTube's "inauthentic content" rule removes monetization for, and a serious violation on one channel can put the others on the account at risk.
kit_edit.replace_with: Uploading templated videos to ten at once is what YouTube's "inauthentic content" rule removes monetization for. YouTube's spam policy, which covers "coordinated networks of channels", can also end in termination. Strikes on one channel can cost all your channels their monetization, and if one channel is terminated, YouTube's rules bar you from using any of your other channels.

findings.topic: YPP entry thresholds rise on Feb 1, 2027
findings.official_quote: Starting Feb. 1, 2027, YPP entry thresholds for new creators are changing to 8,000 qualified watch hours in the last 365 days, or 20M qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days, in addition to still needing 1k subscribers. If you are already in YPP, your status is not impacted by this update.
findings.applies: The current numbers on the YPP page are "Get 1,000 subscribers with 4,000 qualified watch hours in the last 12 months, or" "Get 1,000 subscribers with 10 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days." (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/72851). Channels started now (Nov 2026) won't reach those before Feb 1, 2027, so each channel's goal for ad revenue is 1,000 subscribers plus 8,000 watch hours in 365 days, or 20M Shorts views in 90 days. That is double the long-form hours. The lower tier doesn't change and pays fan funding and Shopping, not ad revenue: "Get 500 subscribers with 3 valid public uploads in the last 90 days, and 3,000 qualified watch hours in the last 12 months, or" "Get 500 subscribers with 3 valid public uploads in the last 90 days, and 3 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days" (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/13429240). Each channel qualifies and is reviewed on its own ("Our automated systems and human reviewers will review your channel as a whole", 72851).
findings.action: Update every growth or monetization plan that gives new channels 1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 hours or 10M Shorts views. Use 1,000 subscribers plus 8,000 hours or 20M Shorts views. Treat the 500-subscriber tier as the first milestone, and focus effort on fewer channels so each one can reach 8,000 hours.

findings.topic: AI personas giving advice: official, not just reported
findings.official_quote: This policy refers to channels that use AI-generated personas to deliver information on sensitive topics. This includes any content that presents itself as a human expert providing advice to viewers on topics such as health, legal issues, finances, or politics. To protect viewers who may be confused or otherwise negatively impacted by this content, channels uploading this content will not be allowed to monetize.
findings.applies: The kit's shared notes call this "reported". It is YouTube's own written policy, and it applies to the whole channel, not one video. It covers channel 8 (legal and insurance) and any money channel, such as Stick Ledger's personal finance scripts, if an AI voice or character presents itself as an expert giving advice.
findings.action: Keep finance and legal channels to explaining ideas, without an AI 'expert' character giving advice. Use your own voice or a plainly labelled narrator, and never present the narrator as a lawyer, adviser or doctor.

kit_edit.quote: AI personas giving advice on money, health or law are reported as not monetizable.
kit_edit.replace_with: YouTube's monetization policy says channels whose AI personas present themselves as human experts giving advice on health, legal issues, finances or politics will not be allowed to monetize.

findings.topic: How many channels one Google Account can have
findings.official_quote: You can manage up to 100 channels from one Google Account.
findings.applies: Ten Brand Account channels under one Google Account is well within the limit. YouTube's feature table (https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/9890437) lists "Add additional channels to your account" as a feature you can't use without verification. Phone verification unlocks it.
